price_range: Sunday brunch 6,500 TL per person with soft drinks; 7,700 TL with wine, beer and cocktails, VAT included (2026)
reservation: Book through the hotel's CheckandPlace listing or +90 212 326 46 20. Sunday brunch goes first.
notes: Sharing plates in the Çırağan Palace Kempinski. It revived the long-missed Sunday brunch tradition.
verdict: Eight months old, and honest about what it is: an international sharing-plates brand parked in the best-sited hotel on the Bosphorus. The draw is the Sunday brunch, which revives the Çırağan tradition — open buffet, live chef stations, a separate dessert room, 12:30 to 16:00 — at 6,500 TL a head with soft drinks or 7,700 TL with wine, beer and cocktails, VAT included. It carries no MICHELIN mark, and it opened only days before the Türkiye 2026 selection was announced on 4 December 2025, far too late to have been assessed. Read the absence as timing rather than judgement, for now.
caveat: TWO CORRECTIONS. This guide previously pinned it at 41.03627 / 29.093512 — roughly 7 km away, on the Asian shore near Kandilli. And it carried an April 2026 opening, which was in fact the publication date of a design-press write-up: Turkish coverage had the room open by 2 December 2025 and Kempinski announced the opening itself that month. No coordinate is given here now, because the only figure we could source is Wikipedia's arcminute-rounded point for the palace, which is not a street-level geocode and this guide pins only those. The address and phone are verified against the hotel. No chef is named by the hotel or in any release between December 2025 and June 2026. Closed Mondays except for breakfast, and brunch at 6,500–7,700 TL is a special-occasion outlay that books out first; under-5s eat free, 6 to 11 at half price.

name: Namlı Gurme
neighborhood: Karaköy, Beyoğlu — two minutes off the waterfront
address: Kemankeş Mahallesi, Mumhane Caddesi, Atilla İş Hanı No: 6/A, Karaköy, Beyoğlu
notes: This is the single most efficient provisioning stop on the European side, and its own shop publishes the numbers, VAT included: çemeni sıyrılmış pastırma, the fenugreek crust scraped back, ₺5,400/kg; an 850 g kangal sucuk made from 100% beef in the house's own workshop, ₺1,836; Gelibolu eski kaşar ₺1,690/kg and Kars Göle eski kaşar ₺1,080/kg; Erzincan tulum ₺1,180/kg, Van otlu peynir ₺1,490/kg, Ezine beyaz peynir ₺598 a block, Balıkesir buffalo butter ₺576 for 450 g. On the dry side: kuru sele olives ₺780/kg, Ayvalık kırma yeşil ₺590/kg, a litre of Makaron olive oil ₺1,080, 330 g of tahin ₺240, Elazığ mulberry pekmez ₺350 and nar ekşisi ₺350 for 350 ml. Honey is the outlier — Hakkari karakovan comb honey ₺4,200 — and these are the online-store figures checked in August 2026, so the counter can differ. The hours are the real advantage: Monday to Sunday, 07:00 to 22:00.

name: Kurukahveci Mehmet Efendi
neighborhood: Eminönü, Fatih — at the corner of the Spice Bazaar
address: Tahmis Sokağı 66, Eminönü 34116, İstanbul (branch: Söğütlüçeşme Caddesi 12, Kadıköy 34714)
notes: The house is in its 155th year — its own site runs the anniversary as "155. YIL" and its official channel carries the founding date in the handle — and it is still at Tahmis Sokağı 66, in the purpose-built block the company credits to the architect Zühtü Başar. There are only three shops in the whole city, all confirmed on the company's own contact pages: the Eminönü merkez, a Sirkeci branch, and Kadıköy at Osmanağa Mahallesi, Söğütlüçeşme Caddesi 12 — anything sold as Mehmet Efendi anywhere else is retail packaging, not the counter grind. The queue is long, moves fast, and almost everyone in it buys the same thing: Türk kahvesi ground to order and handed over still warm. The company does not publish shop hours on its own site, which is worth knowing before you cross the Golden Horn for it.

name: Karaköy Güllüoğlu
address: Kemankeş Karamustafa Paşa Mah., Kemankeş Cad. No:67, 34425 Karaköy — Beyoğlu
notes: The dynasty's origin is documented outside the family's own marketing: baklava was introduced to Gaziantep in 1871 by Çelebi Güllü, who had learned the recipe from a Syrian chef in Damascus. The city's version was registered as a Turkish geographical indication in 2008 and became Antep Baklavası, a Protected Geographical Indication under the European Commission, in 2013 — the first Turkish product to receive one. This house dates itself to 1843 and puts Nadir Güllü at the counter as "the fifth generation representative of a family that has been making baklava since 1843," trained by his father and master Hacı Mustafa Güllü. The decisive fact is the smallest one: their contact page lists a single shop, Kemankeş Caddesi 67, and OpenStreetMap records the same telephone the house publishes, +90 850 308 45 45, against hours running to one in the morning.

name: Tarihi Kadıköy Çarşısı
neighborhood: Kadıköy, Asian side — five minutes' walk from the ferry pier
address: Güneşlibahçe Sokağı and Serasker Caddesi, Osmanağa, Kadıköy
notes: The market is not a building, it is a grid of short streets behind Söğütlüçeşme, and Güneşlibahçe Sokağı is its spine — OpenStreetMap maps fishmongers at nos. 1–3, a greengrocer at no. 9, butchers, bakeries and a spice counter inside about eighty metres of each other, with more fish and a butcher's row round the corner on Serasker Caddesi. Buy to the Turkish fishing calendar rather than to a shopping list: commercial fishing runs 1 September to 15 April, so palamut lands from September, lüfer through the autumn and hamsi from late autumn into winter, while between mid-April and the end of August almost everything on ice is farmed levrek and çipura or flown in. Fish is chalked per kilo and cleaned at the counter at no charge; produce is priced per kilo too, and the crates behind the stall are usually cheaper than the display. Stall names on this street turn over faster than the trades do, so shop the counter, not the sign — verify any single shop before you make a special trip for it.

name: Agora Meyhanesi 1890
notes: Asteri Dulidis, a Greek sea captain, opened it in 1890; his son Stelyo and then his grandson Hristo Dulidis ran it after him, three generations of one family on one street. The barrel tables are the original format — wine drawn straight off a cask — which is what a meyhane was before anyone made it picturesque. Restored in 2013 by the architect Hakan Kıran, trading seven days. The sign, the family name and the neighbourhood still agree with each other.
verdict: A Greek captain's tavern in Balat — still open, its community long gone.

name: The rakı sofrası
notes: Under the Turkish Food Codex, rakı is suma — grape or raisin distillate — redistilled with Pimpinella anisum in traditional copper pot stills of no more than 5,000 litres, bottled at 40 per cent minimum. Water turns it white: aslan sütü, lion's milk. The order is fixed. Cold mezes first and held a long time, then hot, then the fish. You drink at the speed of the table and never without food. Ordering rakı and eating fast is the visitor's giveaway.
verdict: Not a drink with dinner — a table that paces food across an evening.

name: Çiçek Pasajı
notes: Built in 1876 as the Cité de Péra by the Greek banker Hristaki Zoğrafos, on ground cleared by the 1870 Pera fire that destroyed the Naum Theatre — a Second Empire arcade of European shops and apartments. As Pera declined the shops became rough meyhanes: beer barrels rolled onto the pavement, marble slabs laid across them. It was restored in 1988, and again since. The building came back. The clientele did not.
verdict: The prettiest arcade on İstiklal, and the clearest map of what was taken.

name: WAYANA Wine Bar & Tapas
notes: Moda, and the single most useful room in Istanbul for anyone who thinks Turkish wine means a hotel Cabernet. The house carries labels from 143 Turkish wineries and, as of July 2026, ninety endemic grape varieties — and serves the entire list by the glass, which is the whole point: you can taste eight native grapes in one evening instead of gambling a bottle on one. Tapas alongside, built to pair rather than to fill. Start here and the rest of the guide reads differently.
verdict: Every one of 500-plus labels open by the glass. Nowhere else does this.

name: Lips Wine Bar
address: Teşvikiye, Hacı Emin Efendi Sok., Nişantaşı Apt No:24C, Şişli, İstanbul
notes: One of the two openings that visibly thickened the natural-wine layer this year, tucked into an apartment building on a Teşvikiye side street: a short chef-driven small-plates list against low-intervention pours, and lighting dim enough to hold a table for three hours. Monday to Saturday, five in the afternoon until one in the morning. It is closed on Sundays without exception — the night visitors most often try it, and the reason to check the day before you cross town.
verdict: Nişantaşı's low-lit natural-wine room, small plates, and a hard Sunday shutter.
hot_this_month: Opened in the current wave

name: Öküzgözü & Boğazkere
notes: Öküzgözü, 'bull's eye', comes from the villages around Elazığ and Malatya: violets, red and black plum, soft ripe tannin, medium-bodied and generous, and capable of oak without collapsing. Boğazkere grows down the Tigris from Diyarbakır and is its opposite — dense, structural, aggressively tannic, the name meaning roughly 'throat-scraper'. Blended, the first sands down the second, and that blend is what Turkey exports as its own idea. Order each on its own once, to hear what it was actually contributing.
verdict: The bull's eye and the throat-scraper — Turkey's great red pairing, rarely poured apart.

name: Kalecik Karası
notes: From Kalecik, north-east of Ankara on the Kızılırmak. Pale to medium in colour, red cherry and strawberry, low to moderate tannin — and Turkish drinkers reach almost automatically for Gamay or Pinot Noir to describe it, which tells you exactly what it is for. This is the bottle when the table is eating mezes rather than grilled meat. Serve it cool. In a country whose reputation abroad rests on tannin, it is the standing argument for the other direction.
verdict: The Anatolian red that drinks like Gamay, and was nearly lost.

name: Narince & Emir
notes: Narince is Tokat's grape and its name means 'delicately' — aromatic, medium to full-bodied, with a texture that carries oak without losing the fruit. Emir comes off the volcanic soils of Cappadocia: high acid, mineral and savoury, sharper and more austere than Narince, and the one with real ageing capacity. Between them they cover the entire Turkish white argument, and both are absurdly cheap set against any European equivalent. Emir with fish and raw things, Narince with anything out of a wood oven.
verdict: One means 'delicately'; the other grows on Cappadocian volcanic rock.

name: Papazkarası & Çalkarası
notes: Papazkarası — 'priest's black' — is Thracian, thick-skinned, high in acid and modest in tannin, now vinified as a varietal red, as blanc de noirs and as traditional-method sparkling. Çalkarası comes from the Çal district of Denizli in the inland Aegean and reaches its best as rosé: pale, dry, sharply acidic, tart cherry and pomegranate where a Provençal wine would give melon. Both are summer bottles, both are improving fast, and both are still priced as curiosities rather than as serious wine.
verdict: The two that make the country's best rosés, from opposite ends of it.

name: Nayah
notes: Kırtasiyeci Sokak in Kadıköy, running fifteen years and more, and narrow in the best possible way — it does one thing. Roots reggae, dub and dancehall on sound-system logic rather than DJ-set logic, live bands most weekends, and a dancefloor on the top level with the neighbourhood spread out beneath it. If the listening bars are about sitting still and hearing detail, this is the same obsession with sound pushed in the opposite direction.
verdict: The only terrace in Turkey given over entirely to reggae, dub and dancehall.

name: Dama
notes: Şakayık Sokak in Teşvikiye, and its own line is 'café by day, hi-fi by night'. Mornings are filter coffee, breakfast and laptops on a quiet side street; the evening hands the room to vinyl through a system somebody clearly spent real money on, with an open kitchen, ceramic surfaces and shelves of records. Short seasonal cocktail list, small plates. The cleanest single example of the format Istanbul has adopted faster than anywhere else.
verdict: Filter coffee by day, vinyl through serious speakers once the light goes.
hot_this_month: New in the current wave

name: Frankhan
notes: Opened in 2023 by the Selectist team inside a Karaköy han, running house, electro and live electronic on the main floor. Behind it sits the Sound Room, a far smaller space held within the original walls of the han. Check which of the two rooms is open on the night; they do not always run together.
verdict: A Karaköy han, a main floor for dancing, and a second, much smaller room behind it.

name: FLUX
notes: An RX Istanbul project in a modular room that scales from fifty to five hundred indoors plus a two-hundred-capacity terrace, on Funktion-One. The programming split is explicit and worth planning around: Fridays run house, groove-led and rhythmic; Saturdays go techno, deeper and harder. The opening season, autumn 2025, carried Ben Klock, Anja Schneider, Cormac, Setaoc Mass and Stef Mendesidis; 2026 has run to Rødhåd, Regal, Tommy Four Seven, Adriana Lopez and FJAAK. This is the serious room, and it is a long way north — budget for the taxi.
verdict: Funktion-One in Maslak, and the two nights are deliberately not the same night.

name: NOH Radio Bar / NOH Extended
notes: Two rooms and one idea. The Radio Bar in Firuzağa is compact enough that the sound spills onto the pavement and the crowd stands outside with it — electronic, house, trance, visiting DJs, no pretence at a door policy. NOH Extended on Tosbağa Sokak is the late half: multi-level, exhibition space upstairs, club underneath, and the particular mix of underground scene, art crowd and record obsessives that Beyoğlu still assembles better than anywhere across the water.
verdict: So small the music goes out into the street, plus a late annexe.

name: Suma Han
notes: Built in 1923 by the Greek architect Simotas and worked as a rakı distillation plant. Bought in 2003, restored, and reopened in 2009 as offices, artist studios, residences and common rooms with a club floor and genuine acoustics folded in — two stages, techno and psy-trance, plus exhibitions and talks. That the city's clearest case of artists building their own infrastructure sits inside a Greek-built rakı works is not a coincidence this guide is going to let pass.
verdict: A Greek-built rakı distillery, now an artists' building with a club inside.
hot_this_month: With the Biennial in its academy year, spaces like this are where the programming actually is

name: POPSTEL — Stay Local
notes: Not a club so much as a series, run out of a hostel bar on Tomtom Sokak in Galatasaray, and the necessary correction to a city that can feel as though it only plays four-to-the-floor. Stay Local works Y2K hip-hop, UK garage and dark disco to a young local crowd rather than an imported-headliner one, which is the entire premise of the name. Check the dates: the room is only worth the walk when the series is actually on.
verdict: The night that ignores techno entirely: Y2K rap, UK garage, dark disco.

name: The Bank Roof Bar
reservation: Book for sunset
notes: Bankalar Caddesi — Voyvoda Caddesi on the older maps — was the financial centre of the late Ottoman Empire, and the houses that built it were largely Galata's Jewish, Greek and Armenian banking families; the Camondos cut their baroque staircase down the hill to it in the nineteenth century. The banks left for Levent in the 1990s. The hotel took one of their buildings at No. 5, and the terrace looks across the Golden Horn to Hagia Sophia, Topkapı and the Blue Mosque.
verdict: A drink on the roof of the street that financed the Ottoman Empire.

name: Roof106
neighborhood: Galata — atop the Galata Times Hotel, Beyoğlu
notes: The name is the street number. Meşrutiyet Caddesi is the Pera spine — the Pera Palace, the old consulates and The Marmara Pera all stand on it — so two of the city's roofs sit a few hundred metres apart on the same pavement at very different money. From the top of the Galata Times Hotel the line of sight runs over the Golden Horn to the peninsula, with the tower close on the left. Confirm the day as well as the hour: it closes on Tuesdays.
verdict: Named after its own front door: Meşrutiyet Caddesi number 106.

name: Mikla Bar
notes: Mehmet Gürs's restaurant holds a MICHELIN star and occupies the top two floors of The Marmara Pera, but the bar is a separate proposition. It opens at 18:00 and runs to 02:00, has an outdoor terrace and a pool, and does not require the tasting menu — you can sit at it for the price of a cocktail. It is the highest roof on Meşrutiyet Caddesi, which is most of what you are paying for.
verdict: The starred kitchen is downstairs; the terrace will pour you a drink without it.

name: Roof Mezzepotamia
neighborhood: Sirkeci, Fatih — terrace of the Orient Occident Hotel, Autograph Collection
address: Hobyar Mah., Hoca Kasım Köprüsü Sok. No:2, Sirkeci, Fatih, İstanbul
reservation: Book for sunset
notes: It is in Sirkeci, on the historic peninsula, on the terrace of the Orient Occident Hotel — not Karaköy, where a run of English-language listings puts it. The difference is the whole point: from here you look back at Galata instead of out from it, across 270 degrees of the Bosphorus, the Golden Horn and the tower. The name folds mezze into Mesopotamia, and the kitchen runs the seven regions of Turkey. Sirkeci Station, terminus of the Orient Express from 1890, is a few doors away.
verdict: The one every English guide puts on the wrong shore.

name: Sky Karaköy
neighborhood: 9th floor, JW Marriott İstanbul Bosphorus, Karaköy
notes: Ninth floor of the JW Marriott İstanbul Bosphorus, above Karaköy and close enough to Galataport that the cruise ships become part of the view. Stated hours are 17:00 to 01:00 daily. The caveat is not invented: Marriott's own listing for the bar has carried a Seasonally Closed label, which is a hotel group's way of saying the roof shuts when the weather turns. Telephone the hotel before you build an evening around it.
verdict: Ninth floor, the strait wide open — when it is actually open.

name: Manifest Roof
notes: A short walk from the Galata Tower on Şimşir Sokak, and the only roof here that stays open through winter: a glass ceiling holds the Golden Horn in view through rain and cold, when most Galata terraces simply close. The kitchen runs a long Mediterranean and Turkish list — around sixty dishes — rather than a bar menu, so treat it as a dinner room that happens to be on a roof. Its own pages disagree about the hours; confirm when you book.
verdict: The Galata roof that does not shut when the weather turns.
hot_this_month: The summer's new rooftop entry

name: Hood
notes: Twelve floors above Moda on the Kadıköy shore, which puts the European skyline on the far side of the water rather than underneath you: the old-city peninsula, the mouth of the Bosphorus and the Princes' Islands out in the Marmara, in one sweep. Service runs 15:00 to 23:00 and the dress code is smart casual. Getting there is a ferry crossing at dusk, which is arguably the better half of the evening.
verdict: The Asian side's roof, and the only one that sees everything at once.

name: What a drink costs up there
notes: Budget roughly 600 to 900 TL for a cocktail at a mainstream hotel rooftop in 2026. The marquee addresses sit above that band — current listings for the best-known Karaköy and Pera terraces run 1,000 to 1,200 TL a cocktail, The Bank Roof Bar among them. The gap between the two bands is the view, not the liquor.
verdict: You are buying the sightline. The drink is incidental.

name: The hour
notes: Turkey abolished daylight saving on 7 September 2016 and has stayed on UTC+3 ever since, an hour ahead of its own longitude. The effect on a roof is direct: mid-August sunset falls around 20:05, with the golden hour from about 19:25 and blue light holding to about 20:35. By midwinter the same moment arrives just before 17:40. Arrive at least forty-five minutes early if you want a table on the rail.
verdict: Turkey never puts its clocks back, so the light lasts absurdly late.

name: The season
notes: An Istanbul rooftop is a summer business. Terraces glass themselves in, cut their hours or close outright from about November, and the listings do not always keep up — Sky Karaköy carries a Seasonally Closed label on its own group's site, and Manifest advertises its glass ceiling precisely because staying open through the cold is unusual here. Between November and March, telephone the venue on the day. A confirmed booking is not proof the roof is trading.
verdict: Half these roofs simply are not there in winter.

name: Moda
notes: The headland below Kadıköy, laid out in the late nineteenth century when Greek, Armenian and Levantine families built wooden summer houses down the lanes to the water. Their churches — Hagia Triada among them — still hold services; their congregations are a fraction of what they were. The Vedat Tek ferry pier of about 1917 has been restored as a book café and public library, and the coast path around the point is the best free hour on the Asian side. Walk it westward into the sunset.
verdict: Wooden villas built by three communities, and the pier that outlived them.

name: Yeldeğirmeni
notes: Named for the flour mills that once ground for the palace, and settled since the fifteenth century by Armenians, Greeks and Jews — a handful of families remain. It was the first quarter in Kadıköy to build apartment blocks instead of wooden houses, and several of the originals still stand on their streets. A mural programme covered the gable walls a decade ago; the coffee and the quieter rooms followed. Coffee Manifesto holds this end of the district. Go in the morning.
verdict: Windmills, railway workers, and the first apartment blocks on this shore.

name: Üsküdar
notes: Megaran settlers again, this time calling it Chrysopolis, the golden city. Ottoman Üsküdar was the terminus of the Anatolian caravan routes and, for much of the Ottoman period, the point at which the Surre caravan left the mainland carrying the sultan's gifts to Mecca; the regular caravan ended in 1915. That made it Muslim, settled and sober while the rest of the city was mixed and licensed — which is why the lokantas here are superb and the meyhanes essentially absent.
verdict: The gold city, and where the caravans set out for Mecca.

name: Beyoğlu / Pera
notes: Pera is Greek for beyond — the quarter across the Golden Horn from the old city. Foreigners won the right to buy property here in 1867 and built the Grand Rue de Péra with it: arcades, apartment houses and hotels in every style the century could supply. The Cité de Péra of 1876 became the Çiçek Pasajı, its elegant shops turned into rough meyhanes with barrels for tables.
verdict: The avenue was called Grand Rue de Péra, and it was not Turkish.

name: Cihangir
notes: Named for the mosque Sinan built in 1559 for Şehzade Cihangir, Süleyman's son, dead at twenty-two; the present building is an 1889 replacement after repeated fires and earthquakes. The slope below Taksim became the writers-and-cats quarter in the 1990s and has held that register better than most gentrified districts manage. Two rooms from this guide sit here: Casius, cooking Antakya food and carrying a 2026 Bib Gourmand, and Østre, the oyster and raw bar that opened this year.
verdict: A dead prince's mosque, then the writers, now the small serious rooms.

name: Nişantaşı
notes: A nişan taşı is an inscribed stele recording a record shot: Selim III's here dates from 1790–91, Mahmud II's from 1811. Mahmud II then encouraged settlement and the archery ground became the city's grandest residential grid. It is not a cooking quarter. It is a drinking and listening one — Lips for natural wine, and June and Dama in Teşvikiye next door, the second a café that turns hi-fi bar after dark.
verdict: Named for the stones that recorded how far a sultan's arrow flew.

name: Karaköy and Galata
notes: Galata was a colony of the Republic of Genoa from 1267 to 1453 — walled, self-governing, and topped by the tower it finished in 1348. Five centuries later the banker Abraham Salomon Camondo cut his baroque staircase down to Bankalar Caddesi so he could walk from his house to his bank. Galataport reopened this waterfront to the public in 2021. Neolokal holds a star above it; the roof bars hold the view.
verdict: A Genoese city-state with its own walls, now the cruise front.

name: Balat
notes: The name is probably from palation, palace, for the Blachernae ruins on the hill above. Sephardic and Romaniote families lived here for five centuries; the Ahrida synagogue, founded in the 1430s by Jews from Ohrid, is one of the oldest in the city and still in use. Agora Meyhanesi, which dates itself to 1890, is the reason to be here after dark. The painted staircases draw a queue by mid-morning, so do the lanes first and the photograph never.
verdict: Five centuries of Jewish Istanbul, sold now as a colour photograph.

name: Fener
notes: Phanar, the lighthouse, named the quarter and then the Phanariots — the Greek families who supplied the Ottoman state its dragomans, its interpreters and its Danubian princes. The Ecumenical Patriarchate is still here, and above it stands the Phanar Greek Orthodox College, the Red Castle, built 1881–83 by the architect Konstantinos Dimadis at a recorded cost of 17,210 Ottoman gold pounds. The school itself opened in 1454, the year after the conquest. It has outlasted the community it was built to teach.
verdict: The first throne of Orthodoxy, and a red school on the hill.

name: Arnavutköy
notes: Byzantine Mega Revma, the great current, for the water that runs fastest along this bank. Mehmed II resettled Albanians here in 1468 and the Turkish name followed, but the village stayed heavily Greek into the twentieth century, with Armenian and Jewish families beside them. It grew the Ottoman strawberry — small, less sweet than the modern berry, intensely scented — on forty hectares of hillside that are now streets. The bay-windowed wooden yalı are the best surviving row on the European shore. Tam Ocakbaşı cooks here.
verdict: The great current, an Albanian name, and a strawberry that lost its fields.

name: Bebek
notes: The name means baby, and the bay is the calmest water on the European shore, which is why the yalı here belong to people who can afford calm. The white art nouveau pile on the front was built 1899–1901 for Emine Valide Pasha, mother of the last Khedive of Egypt; it became the Egyptian embassy and was later downgraded to a consulate once the capital moved to Ankara. The whole city's demotion, in one building.
verdict: A palace demoted to a consulate when the capital left.

name: Tarabya
notes: Byzantine Pharmakia — poison, after the Medea legend — until it was renamed Therapeia, the cure, for its springs; tradition credits Archbishop Atticus, some time between 406 and 425. It became the summer address of the embassies. Abdülhamid II gave the German one its plot in 1880; the residence went up between 1885 and 1887 and has run since 2011 as an artists' residency. The bay below is a fish-restaurant row, and Arogan, with Burak Zafer cooking, opened above it this year.
verdict: Poison, renamed cure, then rented to ambassadors.

name: Eminönü to Kadıköy
notes: The line traces back to the Şirket-i Hayriye of 1851, the Ottoman empire's first joint-stock company; the boats today are run by Şehir Hatları, municipal since 2006 and working 32 lines from 53 piers. Take the open deck, order tea from the tray that never spills, and watch the old city separate from Galata as you pull out. It is transport rather than a tour, which is exactly why it is worth doing.
verdict: The commute that happens to be the best twenty minutes in the city.

name: Karaköy or Eminönü to Üsküdar
notes: Üsküdar was Chrysopolis, founded by colonists from Megara in the seventh century BC, and for centuries the point at which Asia began: the caravan roads east and the pilgrim road to Mecca started from this shore. The Maiden's Tower stands offshore — a Byzantine tower of 1110 on a rock the Athenians had already used as a customs post, rebuilt repeatedly since; what you see is Ottoman. Sinan's Mihrimah Sultan mosque sits above the pier and his small Şemsi Paşa mosque almost in the water. Cross back westward at dusk and the European skyline lights up in front of you.
verdict: The shortest hop to Asia — take it back westward with the sun going down.

name: The Golden Horn line — Üsküdar to Eyüpsultan
price_range: ~50 min end to end · hop off
notes: The Haliç line runs Üsküdar, Karaköy, Kasımpaşa, Fener, Balat, Hasköy, Ayvansaray, Sütlüce, Eyüpsultan — which is to say it stops at the door of every walk in the next group. The Golden Horn is 7.5 km long and was an industrial sewer within living memory; the clean-up through the 1980s and 1990s is the reason you can now sit on deck and enjoy it. Ride to the top, walk, and come back by boat.
verdict: One boat, nine piers, and the door of every walk in the next group.

name: Kuzguncuk's one street
notes: İcadiye Caddesi runs a few hundred metres up from the water, and along it stand a mosque, the Bet Yaakov synagogue — conventionally dated 1878 and probably older — an Armenian church and Greek Orthodox ones. Sephardic Jews settled here after the expulsions from Spain; the oldest Jewish gravestone in the neighbourhood is dated 1562. The community thinned after 1948 and emptied fast after the 1955 pogrom, replaced by migrants from the Black Sea coast. One street, the whole argument.
verdict: A mosque, a synagogue and a church on the same short road.

name: Moda and the Kadıköy sea walk
notes: Moda became fashionable from the 1870s as a summer quarter for Greek, Armenian and Levantine families, which is why Greek Orthodox, Anglican and Catholic churches and the 1870 Lycée Saint-Joseph still stand among the apartment blocks. The pier building dates from 1917 and was restored in 2022. Walk out to Moda Burnu, sit on the grass with everyone else and watch the sun drop behind the Historic Peninsula. The nostalgia tram loops back into Kadıköy.
verdict: The flat seafront the Asian side actually uses, pointed at the sunset.

name: Fener — the Patriarchate and the Red Castle
notes: The Ecumenical Patriarchate has sat here since about 1600, and the Phanariot Greeks of this quarter supplied the Ottoman state its dragomans and, between 1711 and 1821, the governors of Wallachia and Moldavia. Above it rises the vast red-brick Phanar Greek Orthodox College, which now has almost no pupils, and that is the plainest measure of what happened here. Nearby, St Mary of the Mongols is the only Byzantine church in the city that has never stopped being a Greek Orthodox place of worship; the firmans of Mehmed II and Bayezid II granting it to the Greek community still hang there.
verdict: Orthodoxy's senior see, on a back street, behind an iron gate.

name: The iron church of St Stephen
notes: The Bulgarians broke from the Greek Patriarchate in 1870 and wanted a church of their own. The Ottoman Armenian architect Hovsep Aznavur drew it on an iron frame because the ground here is soft; the Austrian firm R. Ph. Waagner cast some 500 tonnes of parts in Vienna between 1893 and 1896 and shipped them down the Danube and across the Black Sea. Consecrated 8 September 1898, restored 2011 to 2018. A whole church made of metal.
verdict: A church cast in Vienna, shipped down the Danube, bolted together here.

name: Balat — Ahrida and the Jewish quarter
notes: Bayezid II opened the city to Jews fleeing the Spanish Inquisition after 1492 and Balat became the centre of Istanbul's Jewish life, with eighteen synagogues at its height. Ahrida was founded in the fifteenth century by Jews from Ohrid; its wooden bimah is built in the shape of a boat's prow, and Sabbatai Zevi prayed here — the only Istanbul synagogue where he did. He had proclaimed himself the Messiah at Smyrna at Rosh Hashanah in 1665, and on reaching Constantinople in February 1666 he was arrested on the order of the grand vizier Köprülüzade Fazıl Ahmed Pasha. Three synagogues still work. B
verdict: Eighteen synagogues once; three still working, one with a bimah shaped like a prow.

name: Eyüpsultan and the hill above it
notes: Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, a companion of the Prophet, died during the Arab siege of Constantinople in the 670s. His tomb was declared rediscovered after 1453, and the mosque raised over it became the place where each new sultan was girded with the Sword of Osman. It is a working pilgrimage site, so dress for it and avoid Friday midday. Above, the cemetery climbs to the Pierre Loti café, named for the French novelist and reached by cable car.
verdict: A pilgrimage mosque, a cemetery up the slope, and a cable car to the view.

name: Büyükada by ferry
notes: The Byzantines exiled inconvenient royals here, which is where the name comes from. A 1912 census counted roughly 10,250 Greeks to 670 Turks across the nine islands; this was a Greek, Armenian and Jewish summer world and it is not one now. Private cars are still banned. The horse phaetons have gone too: an outbreak of glanders among the horses finished them, and an Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality council decision of 16 January 2020 ended the phaeton era for good, with electric vehicles taking over the same summer.
verdict: Five and a half square kilometres with no engine noise in them.

name: The Monastery of St George
notes: Aya Yorgi sits at the island's highest point, 203 metres up. A chapel of 1751 stood here; the present cut-stone church was begun in 1905 and finished in 1909. The origin story — icons buried during a medieval sack and rediscovered after a shepherd's dream — is the standard one for a Greek shrine. What is not standard is the crowd: on 23 April, St George's day, thousands climb the path, and a great many of them are Muslim.
verdict: A steep climb that Muslims and Christians make together on the saint's day.

name: The Prinkipo Orphanage
notes: Alexandre Vallaury designed it in 1898 for the Wagons-Lits company as the Prinkipo Palace, a hotel and casino for Orient Express passengers. Abdülhamid II refused the licence; a Greek banker's wife bought it and gave it to the Patriarchate, and it opened as an orphanage on 21 May 1903. Turkish authorities forced it shut on 21 April 1964, the year of the expulsions. Confiscated in 1997, returned after Strasbourg ruled against Turkey.
verdict: Europe's largest wooden building, twenty thousand square metres of it, empty since 1964.

name: Heybeliada and the closed seminary
notes: The Theological School of Halki opened on 1 October 1844 on the hill above Heybeliada and turned out close to a thousand priests, bishops and patriarchs. In 1971 Turkish legislation banning private higher education closed it, and it has taken no student since — though Ankara and the Patriarchate announced in 2026 that it will reopen. American presidents and the EU have pressed for that for decades. The monastery keeps the building, the library and the view. Get off one island early.
verdict: The school that trained a thousand priests, closed by a law about colleges.

name: The long ferry to Anadolu Kavağı
notes: The long Şehir Hatları service runs from Eminönü to Anadolu Kavağı at the northern mouth of the Bosphorus, calling at Sarıyer and Rumeli Kavağı, and holds at the top long enough for lunch before turning back. Above the village stands Yoros Castle, fortified under the late Byzantines, Ottoman from 1391, lost to Genoa in 1414 for forty years — which is why everyone calls it the Genoese castle — then refortified by Mehmed II.
verdict: The whole strait end to end, on a commuter boat with a lunch stop.

name: Belgrad Forest
notes: The name is literal: Süleyman deported thousands of Serbs from Belgrade to the capital in 1521, and the village they were settled in named the forest. Two Ottoman systems ran through it — the sixteenth-century Kırkçeşme network upgraded by Sinan, and the eighteenth-century Taksim one — and their dams and aqueducts, among them the Maglova aqueduct and the Mahmud I arch of 1732, still stand among the sessile oaks. Some 5,500 hectares, with a 6.5 km running loop.
verdict: The oak forest north of the city, and the waterworks that supplied Ottoman Istanbul.

name: Hagia Sophia
notes: Justinian's church was inaugurated on 27 December 537, built in five years and ten months by Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus. The first dome fell in the earthquake of 7 May 558; Isidore the Younger rebuilt it higher and steeper by 562, and that is the dome overhead. Cathedral for nine centuries, mosque from 1453, museum from 1935, mosque again since July 2020.
verdict: The dome came down once already, and the one overhead is the replacement.

name: Chora — Kariye Mosque
notes: Theodore Metochites, Grand Logothete under Andronikos II, paid for the mosaics and frescoes between about 1315 and 1321 and had himself worked into the panel above the door, handing the church over to Christ. He later fell from power and died as a monk inside it. Converted to a mosque in the early sixteenth century, made a museum in 1945, returned to worship and reopened on 6 May 2024 after four years of restoration. The narthex cycles are all visible; the figural mosaics in the prayer hall are veiled.
verdict: The finest Byzantine mosaic cycle anywhere, and three panels of it are behind curtains.

name: Süleymaniye Mosque
notes: Begun 1550, finished 1557, and never only a mosque: it came with four madrasas, a medical school, a hospital, a soup kitchen, a caravanserai and a hamam. Süleyman lies in the garden tomb, Hürrem Sultan in hers of 1558, and Sinan in a small tomb at the corner of the wall he built. Above the entrance he set a chamber that drew oil-lamp smoke off the walls; the collected soot went to the palace calligraphers.
verdict: Sinan piped the lamp smoke into one room and turned the soot into ink.

name: Topkapı Palace
notes: Mehmed II ordered construction from 1459; the palace was finished around 1478 and governed the empire until the court moved to Dolmabahçe in 1856. The Chamber of the Sacred Relics has held its collection since 1517, when Selim I took Cairo and the caliphate came north — and the practice of recitation came with it, kept now by a rota of readers through opening hours. In the Treasury: the Topkapı dagger and the eighty-six-carat Spoonmaker's Diamond.
verdict: The Quran is read aloud, all day, in the room that has held the relics since 1517.

name: Basilica Cistern
notes: Justinian's reservoir was built around 532 beneath a public basilica, which is where the name comes from. Three hundred and thirty-six columns, most of them scavenged from older buildings, carried water to the Great Palace above. In the north-west corner two carved Medusa heads serve as column bases, one laid sideways, one inverted, with no surviving explanation for either. It reopened in July 2022 after five years of restoration and seismic strengthening; management passed to the state foundations body in June 2026, which briefly closed it.
verdict: Two Medusa heads used as furniture, one on her side, one upside down.

name: Istanbul Archaeological Museums
notes: Osman Hamdi Bey excavated the royal necropolis at Sidon in 1887 and brought back a Pentelic marble sarcophagus with its painted surfaces still partly legible — Macedonian and Persian figures fighting in colour. The museum he founded around the find opened on 13 June 1891 and holds roughly a million objects, among them two of the three tablets of the Kadesh treaty of about 1259 BC, the oldest known peace treaty; the United Nations hangs a copy in New York.
verdict: The painter who dug up the Alexander Sarcophagus then built a museum around it.

name: Istanbul Modern
notes: Founded in 2004 as Türkiye's first museum of modern and contemporary art, it started in a Karaköy warehouse, moved out in 2018, and returned to the same stretch of waterfront on 4 May 2023 in Renzo Piano's first building in the country. The aluminium facade is cut to catch the strait's light. On the roof a terrace stands above a shallow reflecting plane, so the water on the building and the water below run together. Semiha Berksoy's retrospective closes 6 September 2026.
verdict: A viewing terrace hovering over a sheet of water covering the whole roof.

name: Pera Museum
notes: The building opened in 1893 as the Bristol, one of the Pera hotels that took Orient Express traffic alongside the Pera Palace and the Tokatlıyan. Its facade was kept and everything behind it rebuilt as galleries; the Suna and İnan Kıraç Foundation opened the museum on 8 June 2005. The anchor is Osman Hamdi Bey's The Tortoise Trainer, painted in 1906 and bought at auction in December 2004 for a sum that was then a record for a Turkish work.
verdict: An 1893 hotel that now owns the record-breaking Turkish painting.

name: SALT Galata
notes: Alexandre Vallaury finished the Imperial Ottoman Bank's headquarters on Bankalar Caddesi in 1892, and the bank held the building until 1999. SALT took it in November 2011 and made it free: galleries, an open research library, a café and bookshop at street level, and the Ottoman Bank archive covering 145 years downstairs.
verdict: The Imperial Ottoman Bank's head office, and it costs nothing to walk in.

name: Zeki Müren
notes: Born in Bursa, schooled in Istanbul, he entered the State Academy of Fine Arts in 1950 and made his first live broadcast on Istanbul Radio on 1 January 1951. He then held the stage at the Maksim gazino in Taksim for eleven years — the big-room, orchestra-backed successor to the meyhane's fasıl nights. A sequinned jacket from 1958, a miniskirt from 1970, and no loss of affection from a conservative public. He collapsed and died at a TRT ceremony on 24 September 1996, leaving everything to two charitable foundations.
verdict: Turkey's most beloved voice belonged to its most flamboyant man, and nobody minded.

name: Prinkipo Greek Orthodox Orphanage
notes: Alexandre Vallaury — the architect of the Ottoman Bank — built it in 1898 for the Wagons-Lits company, which ran the Orient Express, as a hotel and casino. Abdülhamid II refused the operating permit. In 1903 Eleni Zarifi bought it and gave it to the Ecumenical Patriarchate, which ran it as an orphanage for Greek children until Turkish authorities forced it shut on 21 April 1964. Twenty thousand square metres of timber have stood open to the weather since. Title was returned in 2012; a restoration partnership was signed in June 2026.
verdict: Europe's largest wooden building, shut by the state in 1964 and empty since.

name: Yenikapı — the dig that held up the railway
notes: Salvage excavation at Yenikapı ran from 2004 to 2013 and held the Marmaray project up for years. It exposed the Theodosian Harbour and thirty-seven shipwrecks of the fifth to eleventh centuries, the largest group of medieval ships ever found on a single site. Below the harbour floor came something much older: dwelling foundations, burials and human footprints from roughly 8,500 years ago, when the Sea of Marmara was still a lake. Sixty thousand objects in all.
verdict: Digging the Bosphorus rail tunnel turned up a settlement 8,500 years old.

name: Halfdan's runes
notes: In 1964 a runic inscription about twenty-three centimetres long was found scratched into the marble parapet of Hagia Sophia's upper south gallery. Only the ending, -ftan, is legible; runologists read it as Halfdan and reconstruct the ordinary Norse formula behind it — Halfdan carved these runes. He would have been one of the Varangians, the Norse and later Anglo-Saxon mercenaries who guarded Byzantine emperors from the late tenth century. A second name, Ári, surfaced in 1975.
verdict: A Varangian guardsman got bored during a service and carved his name.

name: Tünel
notes: The French engineer Eugène-Henri Gavand built it to solve exactly one problem: the climb from the port at Galata to the merchant quarter at Pera. It opened on 17 January 1875, which makes it the second-oldest underground urban railway in the world after the London Underground of 1863. Five hundred and seventy-three metres of it, about sixty of them vertical. It ran on steam until the renovation that closed the line in 1968; electrified and reopened in 1971, it is still doing the only job it was built for.
verdict: Twelve years after London, the second underground railway on earth — 573 metres.

name: The Obelisk of Theodosius
notes: The granite was cut for Thutmose III and raised at Karnak, its inscriptions marking his campaign to the Euphrates around 1450 BC. Theodosius I had it shipped from Egypt and re-erected on the spine of the Hippodrome in 390 AD. It lost length in transit, so what stands is the upper section, 18.5 metres of it, on a marble base carved in Constantinople showing the emperor watching the races from his box. Nothing else in the city comes close in age.
verdict: Already eighteen centuries old when Constantinople put it up.

name: The Black Russian
notes: Frederick Bruce Thomas was born in Coahoma County, Mississippi in November 1872 to parents who had been enslaved. He reached Moscow by way of London, ran theatres and restaurants there for nineteen years, and fled the revolution to Constantinople. By Vladimir Alexandrov's account he opened Stella in Şişli, then Maxim in Taksim in 1921, and the city heard the foxtrot, the Charleston and live jazz through him. Refused a United States passport and buried in debt, he died in a debtors' prison in June 1928.
verdict: The man who brought jazz to Istanbul was born in Mississippi to freed slaves.

name: Türk kahvesi
notes: Hakem of Aleppo and Şems of Damascus opened Istanbul's first kahvehane in Tahtakale in 1554. Around fifty were counted in the city by the end of Süleyman's reign; Murad IV later banned the drink outright, on the correct assumption that men who sit together talk. UNESCO inscribed Turkish coffee culture in 2013 for the ritual rather than the bean: water first, a sweet alongside, the grounds left in the cup for the fal.
verdict: Two Syrians opened the first coffeehouse here in 1554; the city never recovered.

name: Çay, and the tulip glass
notes: Law 407 of 1924 put tea cultivation on a legal footing at Rize on the wet Black Sea coast; the aim Çaykur records is work and income for the Eastern Black Sea after the First World War. The first large harvest came in 1938, the first factory in 1947. It is served in the ince belli, the thin-waisted glass, held by the rim — and refusing one is close to rude.
verdict: A law of 1924 put tea on the Black Sea coast, and it took over the whole day.

name: Kahvaltı — the word
notes: Kahve altı, 'under coffee', was the small thing eaten before the cup, on the reasoning that Turkish coffee on an empty stomach is punishing. The two words fused into one and the term is first recorded in the 1870s. The meal then outgrew its own name — twenty small plates, three hours, no hurry — and the drink beside it is now tea. The word is a fossil of a coffee city that switched.
verdict: Breakfast here is literally named 'under coffee', and the coffee has since vanished.

name: Çınaraltı, Çengelköy
notes: The name means 'under the plane tree', and the tree is the entire proposition: a vast çınar on the Asian shore at Çengelköy, its canopy over tables facing the water. The garden pours tea and coffee and nothing else — you are expected to bring your own food, and people do, in bags. No music, no backgammon, no nargile, open at any hour. It is the least commercial room in this guide.
verdict: Chairs set under a plane tree said to be nearly a thousand years old.

name: Pierre Loti Kahvesi
notes: Evliya Çelebi knew this hill as the İdris Köşkü picnic ground. By the nineteenth century a coffeehouse called Rabia Kadın stood on it, and the French naval officer Julien Viaud — writing as Pierre Loti — arrived in 1876 and is said to have finished Aziyadé at one of its tables. The hill took his name. Ride the cable car up from Eyüp pier, then walk back down through the Ottoman cemetery: that descent is the reason to come.
verdict: A hilltop coffeehouse from the 1800s, above the graves, looking down the Golden Horn.

name: Moda Aile Çay Bahçesi
notes: A municipal tea garden on the slope above Moda's shore: umbrellas and plastic chairs under tall trees, the Sea of Marmara filling the view with the Princes' Islands on the horizon. Nobody is performing. Grandparents, students and dog-walkers hold tables for hours over tea and tavla, the food runs to sandwiches and toast, and half the room brought its own. This is what the Asian side does with an afternoon.
verdict: The whole of Kadıköy, three generations of it, facing the Marmara over a backgammon board.

name: Çorlulu Ali Paşa Medresesi
notes: Çorlulu Ali Paşa built this medrese in 1708 on the old Divanyolu, the imperial processional road, as a working college. Its two courtyards now hold carpet dealers and one of the city's long-standing nargile and tea gardens — low stools, cushions, glasses arriving without being asked. It is the single good reason to sit down in the old city, which this guide otherwise tells you to eat your way out of.
verdict: A theology college courtyard where the students were replaced by nargile smoke.

name: İnci Pastanesi
notes: İnci opened in the Cercle d'Orient building on İstiklal in the mid-1940s and built the business on one thing: choux balls filled with pastry cream under a chocolate sauce, the profiterol. It is the version every other one in the country is measured against. The shop was evicted in the early 2010s when the building was redeveloped; it went dark for about seventy days and reopened round the corner on Mis Sokak.
verdict: One dessert, one recipe, since the 1940s — then redevelopment moved the whole shop.

name: Markiz (ex-Lebon)
notes: Lebon's patisserie was trading on the Grand Rue from the 1880s and became the salon of Pera, with Pierre Loti and Yahya Kemal among the regulars. Its Art Nouveau faience panels were ordered from France: four seasons commissioned, and only Spring and Autumn survive in the room. When Lebon moved across the street in 1940, Avedis Ohanyan Çakır opened Markiz in the room it left, keeping the tiles. It closed in 1980 and came back, panels and all, in 2003.
verdict: Four Art Nouveau seasons were ordered from France; two are still on the wall.

name: Montag Coffee Roasters
notes: Montag roasts its own and runs rooms in Kadıköy, Moda and Bomonti. The Kadıköy shop is the one to sit in: counter downstairs, a quiet second floor, V60 and cold brew alongside espresso, and the kind of turnover that means the bag you buy was roasted recently. Beans by the bag if you are travelling on.
verdict: Own-roasted beans across three rooms, and the Kadıköy one is where you sit down.

name: Neroli Daylight Kitchen
notes: Neroli is the essential oil pressed from bitter-orange blossom, and the room runs at the same register: daylight, a short seasonal card, handmade croissants, soft breads to its own recipe, gelato. The charcuterie and the cured salmon are made in the kitchen rather than bought in, which is the actual difference here. It shuts at six and does not pretend to become a bar. In a district gone heavily to brunch theatre, that is the correction.
verdict: A kitchen that shuts at six on purpose and makes everything on the plate itself.
hot_this_month: Current daytime opening

name: Mornings in Pera
notes: The room sits in Asmalımescit, the old meyhane grid, and serves the sprawled kahvaltı across the middle of the day rather than for one crowded hour — its own bakery, breakfast running to four in the afternoon. The queue is the price of that: come at nine, or come at three and take the last long table of the day.
verdict: The long Turkish breakfast, run as a proper kitchen rather than a photo set.

name: Ebru — marbling
notes: Pigment ground from earth and mineral, cut with ox gall so it floats, dropped onto water thickened with tragacanth, combed into flowers and stones and waves, then lifted off in one sheet. UNESCO inscribed it in 2014. It was never decorative on its own terms: ebru was made for bookbinders, as endpapers, and as a ground for official documents that could not be forged twice. It lived inside the book trade, not beside it.
verdict: Colour floated on thickened water and lifted onto paper in a single breath.

name: Ebristan — Hikmet Barutçugil
notes: Hikmet Barutçugil, born in Malatya in 1952, trained as a textile designer at the Istanbul State Academy of Fine Arts and turned to marbling in 1977. He opened Ebristan in Salacak, on the Üsküdar shore, in 1996, and works ebru onto cloth, ceramic, glass, wood and wax as well as paper. One pattern carries his name — barut ebrusu, gunpowder marbling. He teaches constantly; sessions are arranged directly rather than booked through a platform.
verdict: The marbler who invented his own pattern and named it gunpowder.

name: Çini — the İznik blue
notes: Çini is Çin — China — with an ending: Ottoman potters were chasing the prestige of imported Chinese blue-and-white, and the language kept the receipt. The İznik body is the trick, up to eighty-five per cent quartz, which is why the glaze reads as lit from behind. Production stopped in the seventeenth century and took the recipe with it. The İznik Foundation, founded in 1993 by the economist Işıl Akbaygil, reverse-engineered the quartz body and fired again from 1995.
verdict: A Turkish word that means Chinese, and it is being honest.

name: Hüsn-i hat — calligraphy
notes: Arabic-script calligraphy written to proportion: every letter measured in rhombic dots laid down by the same reed pen, so a hand is judged on its geometry before its content. The kit is fixed — reed pen, trimming slab, soot ink, paper sized and burnished until the ink cannot bleed. UNESCO inscribed it in 2021. Istanbul is where the Ottoman masters set the proportions the rest of the Islamic world then copied, teacher to pupil, by licence.
verdict: Writing measured in dots, where the shape of the letter is the point.

name: Sakıp Sabancı Museum — the book arts
notes: The Atlı Köşk at Emirgan, built in 1927 by the Italian architect Edouard De Nari, holds what Sakıp Sabancı spent a lifetime buying: five centuries of Ottoman book arts — manuscript Qur'ans, calligraphic panels, albums, hilyes, imperial documents. It began with a single panel by Sultan Mahmud II. The family handed the house and the collection to Sabancı University in 1998 on a forty-nine-year lease, and the museum opened in 2002. This is where hüsn-i hat stops being a description.
verdict: Five hundred years of Ottoman hands, inside a 1927 villa on the Bosphorus.

name: Caferağa Medresesi
notes: Mimar Sinan built this medrese for Cafer Ağa in 1559, in the reign of Süleyman the Magnificent, immediately behind Hagia Sophia. Since 1989 the Türk Kültürüne Hizmet Vakfı has run it as a working crafts school: ebru, hüsn-i hat, tezhip gilding, çini and ceramic, miniature, stained glass, jewellery, felt and weaving, taught in the old student cells around the courtyard. Full courses run over months; shorter sessions exist for visitors. Ask at the gate.
verdict: Sinan's medrese behind Hagia Sophia, still teaching the crafts in its cells.

name: Kapalıçarşı — the Grand Bazaar
notes: Mehmed II began it within three years of the conquest; its stone bedesten for cloth and gems was finished by 1461, and it grew into sixty-one covered streets and more than four thousand shops across 30,700 square metres. Every lane was a guild, and the street names are the surviving record of trades that have since left them: the main artery, Kalpakçılar Caddesi, is Hatmakers' Street, and has not sold a fur hat in living memory. It is now solid gold, end to end.
verdict: Sixty-one streets named for guilds that mostly no longer trade on them.

name: Kalpakçılar Caddesi — the gold
notes: This is the part of the bazaar that is not theatre. Turkish households have held savings in gold for decades because the lira keeps losing value, so the jewellers here are serving locals as much as visitors, and the price is arithmetic rather than performance: the day's gram rate, plus a workmanship charge. Ask for those two numbers separately. The conversation stops being a haggle and becomes a discussion about who made the piece.
verdict: Turks buy gold the way other countries buy government bonds.

name: Zincirli Han
notes: Built in 1708 on the caravanserai plan — shops below, workshops and lodgings above — and historically the han for goldsmithing and jewellery, with carpet and antique dealers alongside. It is the quietest courtyard in the bazaar and still the most working one: metal is melted and copper hammered behind the shopfronts, by ateliers that have run for generations. The master-and-apprentice chain has thinned badly. It has not broken. Go on a weekday morning and stand still.
verdict: The courtyard where the hammering is real and nobody chases you.

name: Carpets and "antiques" — the honest note
notes: Turkish law protects cultural property, and genuinely old carpets, tiles, coins and icons cannot legally leave the country; dealers selling older pieces are expected to hand over museum certification that an item is not an antiquity. Which tells you precisely what the "three-hundred-year-old" rug on the wall is. A reputable seller produces that paperwork unprompted. And turn any rug over — hand-knotted backs are slightly irregular, machine-made ones suspiciously perfect.
verdict: If it is genuinely antique, you are not allowed to take it home.

name: Sahaflar Çarşısı
notes: The booksellers' courtyard between the Grand Bazaar and Beyazıt Mosque stands on the Chartoprateia, the Byzantine paper and book market — the trade has not moved in a thousand years. Sahaf is Arabic: a dealer in written sheets. Ottoman booksellers left the Grand Bazaar for this yard in the eighteenth century; fire took it in the 1950s and it was rebuilt. Honest now — computers and then the internet hollowed the antiquarian trade out, and much of the stock is exam crammers.
verdict: A book market on Byzantine ground, now mostly selling exam crammers.

name: Manol, and who actually built the oud
notes: The Metropolitan Museum, which owns one of his instruments, records Emmanuel Venios — Manol — as Greek, born on Folegandros about 1838 and dead in Istanbul in 1915 or 1916; he had a workshop on İstiklal by about 1870. He is credited with the smaller, higher-tuned instrument the world now calls the Turkish oud, and his are still held to be the finest ever built. The other great maker of the tradition, Onnik Karibyan, working a generation later, was Armenian. The instrument at the centre of Turkish classical music was designed and refined by the communities this city lost.
verdict: The Turkish oud has an inventor, and his name was Manol.

name: Galip Dede Caddesi — the music street
notes: The street falls from Tünel to the Galata Tower and has been the musicians' bazaar for decades: darbuka, davul and frame drums, bağlama and saz, ney and zurna, plus string sellers and repair benches behind the counters. The honest warning is unavoidable — a large share of the bağlamas in the windows are decorative and close to unplayable. Ask to hear one played before you think about buying. If nobody in the shop can play it, that is your answer.
verdict: The whole instrument trade on one downhill street, the good beside the useless.

name: Saz, bağlama, kanun, ud — what the names admit
notes: Saz is simply Persian for "instrument". Bağlama comes from bağlamak, to tie, after the gut frets tied round the neck and slid by hand — which is why the thing plays intervals a piano cannot. Kanun is Greek, kanōn, a rule or measuring rod, because the zither lays down the law of pitch that the singer and the rest of the ensemble tune to. Ud is Arabic al-ʿūd, the wood, and it is where our word lute comes from.
verdict: Four instrument names, four different empires answering at once.

name: Lale Plak
notes: At the Tünel end of the music street, and among the oldest record shops in the city — trading for well over fifty years, with the exact founding year disputed between sources. Hakan Atala's stock runs from Western classical and jazz, signed pressings included, to the 1970s Turkish canon: Barış Manço, Ajda Pekkan, the Anadolu rock era. It is a shop to be served in rather than to browse. Say what you are after and let him pull it.
verdict: Half a century at the top of the music street, run by one ear.

name: Matbah-ı Âmire — the imperial kitchens
notes: The Topkapı kitchens employed more than 800 people and cooked for roughly 4,000 a day. Fire took them in 1574 and Mimar Sinan rebuilt them: ten domed buildings, two rows of twenty wide chimneys. That scale bred a style — measured spicing, rice over bulgur, vegetables cooked in olive oil and eaten cold — which is still what Istanbul means when it calls a dish its own rather than Anatolia's. The rooms now hold 10,700 pieces of Chinese porcelain.
verdict: Eight hundred cooks, four thousand fed daily — and the restraint you still taste.

name: The ocakbaşı
notes: Not an Istanbul invention. The fire counter came up with twentieth-century migration from the south-east and naturalised so completely that visitors now read it as the city's own night food. The order is fixed: liver first, then the skewers, then a lahmacun to close, and the rakı does not stop. A handful of new rooms are reworking the form this year — shorter menus, real wine lists, the same trench. Sit where the smoke goes.
verdict: A bar with a charcoal trench in it, and you sit at the trench.

name: The meyhane table
notes: Alcohol was forbidden to Muslims, so the keeping of a drinking house fell in practice almost entirely to Greeks, Armenians and Jews. That is why the meyhane looks as it does: the long table of cold mezes before the hot, rakı cut with water until it turns white, fasıl players moving between tables. The wealth tax of 1942, the pogrom of September 1955 and the measures of 1964 removed the authors. The form stayed.
verdict: Cold mezes, then hot, then fish — a drinking licence that was never Muslim.

name: Mısır Çarşısı — the Spice Bazaar
notes: Commissioned by Hatice Turhan Sultan, mother of Mehmed IV, and begun in the last months of 1660 after the great fire of that July. It was the arasta of the New Mosque complex: eighty-five shops whose rent maintained the mosque. The name is Egypt — the building went up on revenues from the Ottoman province, and much of what filled it arrived by the same route. Walk the L, buy nothing, and eat in the streets behind it where the traders do.
verdict: Built to fund a mosque, named after the province that paid for it.

name: Kadıköy market streets
notes: Megarian Greeks settled here in 685 BC, a generation before Byzantium; the oracle's line about a capital built opposite the city of the blind is a joke at Chalcedon's expense that has outlasted the city. The Turkish name means village of the judge, for Hızır Bey, Istanbul's first kadı after 1453. Today it is a few sloping lanes of fishmongers, picklers and cheese counters, and the correct way through is to eat at every second stall.
verdict: Chalcedon, the settlement Byzantium's founders were told only the blind would have chosen.

name: Simit
notes: Archival records put simit production in Istanbul at 1525, with weight and price fixed at Üsküdar in 1593 — a regulated staple, not a snack. Evliya Çelebi counted seventy simit bakeries in the 1630s. The word comes from the Arabic for fine flour. Dipped in grape molasses and rolled in sesame before baking, it is chewy hot and cardboard cold, so buy from a tray that is moving. Throwing pieces to the gulls off the ferry is not a tourist habit.
verdict: Made in this city since 1525, and still carried through it on a tray.

name: Balık ekmek
notes: A fillet of oily fish, usually mackerel, grilled and put in a bun with onion and leaves, and it is the city's signature thing eaten standing up. The painted boats at Eminönü serve it off the water and are the image on every postcard; they are also an industrialised operation aimed squarely at visitors. Cross to the Karaköy or Kadıköy side and buy from a counter with a queue of people on their way to work.
verdict: Grilled mackerel in bread — and the famous boats are the version to skip.

name: Midye dolma
notes: The earliest Istanbul record of it is Armenian — an 1888 account describes Armenian cooks preparing large mussels with sheep's-tail fat. The filling is rice with currants, black pepper and red pepper; the lemon is not garnish but the thing that stops the rice drying out. Since the 1960s the carts have been run largely by families from Mardin, whose version runs hotter. You eat until you stop, then you pay for the shells.
verdict: Rice-stuffed mussels counted out one at a time, lemon squeezed over the shell.

name: Kokoreç
notes: Suckling-lamb intestine wrapped around sweetbread, heart and kidney, turned on a horizontal spit and basted with lemon and oil, then chopped fine and packed into half a baguette. The word entered Turkish in 1920, in a short story that described it as a Greek dish; the name goes back to South Slavic, though whether Greek took it via Albanian or the two borrowed it separately is disputed. When EU accession was live in the early 2000s the Turkish press argued about whether Brussels would ban it.
verdict: Lamb intestine wound round offal over charcoal, chopped into bread with oregano.

name: Baklava
notes: The one hard Ottoman fact is a ceremony: on the fifteenth of Ramadan the Sultan sent trays of baklava down to the Janissary barracks in a procession called the Baklava Alayı. The origins are genuinely unsettled — Byzantine koptoplakous, Central Asian Turkic layered breads and the Arab lauzinaj of tenth-century cookbooks all have serious advocates. What is settled is the name: since 2013 Gaziantep Baklavası has carried an EU protected geographical indication.
verdict: Handed to the Janissaries on the fifteenth of Ramadan; claimed by four cuisines since.

name: Pastırma and sucuk
notes: Pastırma comes from bastırma, to press. The Ottomans took a Byzantine cured beef called paston and renamed it; Kayseri became the centre, and an 1893 British Foreign Office report already singled the city out for it. The crust is çemen — crushed fenugreek, cumin, garlic and hot paprika — over meat dried hard. Sucuk is its sausage cousin, garlic-heavy, fried for breakfast. English took pastrami by way of Yiddish, perhaps crossed with salami.
verdict: Air-dried beef under a fenugreek crust — and the word pastrami came from.

name: Lokum
notes: The house of Ali Muhiddin Hacı Bekir dates its Bahçekapı shop to 1777, when its founder came down from Kastamonu; the Oxford Companion to Food notes there is no real evidence for the invention claim, and Tim Richardson has written on how often confectionery dates are commercial rather than historical. The sweet itself is a gel of starch and sugar scented with rosewater, mastic, bergamot or lemon, sometimes loaded with pistachio or walnut. Buy it cut from the tray.
verdict: Starch, sugar and rosewater — and a founding date historians will not sign off.

name: Atatürk Kitaplığı
notes: Sedad Hakkı Eldem — the architect who spent a career folding the Ottoman timber house into modernism — drew this as a culture complex of library, museum and exhibition halls; only the library was ever built. Koç Holding put the building up in 1973 and the collection moved in on 3 March 1981: around 228,000 books, 20,000 periodicals and 10,000 bound volumes of newspapers, alongside manuscripts, maps, albums and postcards. The city runs it, entry is free, and the hours do not move for the weekend — 09:00 to 21:00, every day.
verdict: A free reading room in Beyoğlu, open until nine, seven days a week.

name: SALT Research, SALT Galata
notes: Alexandre Vallaury built this as the headquarters of the Imperial Ottoman Bank, finished in 1892, and the bank worked from it until 1999. Han Tümertekin's conversion reopened the building in November 2011 as SALT Galata, holding the research library and the old Ottoman Bank Museum. Reading costs nothing, but SALT Research is a registered collection rather than a walk-in one: you sign up once and are issued a personal access pass, study areas are bookable in blocks of up to three hours, and nothing circulates. Outside, the stairs cut around 1870–1880 by Abraham Salomon Camondo, of the Ottoman-V
verdict: A bank built for the Galata money, emptied of it, handed to readers.

name: Kronotrop, Cihangir
notes: Kronotrop opened in 2012 as one of the first specialty roasteries in Turkey — its founder, Çağatay Gülabioğlu, was the country's first Q grader — and the Cihangir room is the flagship, on the slope above Tophane where a good share of the city's writers, editors and film people live. It runs 07:00 to 23:30, seven days a week. It is small and it fills, so the etiquette is one long session rather than a whole day at the same table. The chain has since passed forty branches across Turkey and beyond, with very different hours at each, so aim for this room rather than the nearest sign.
verdict: Sixteen hours a day of table, on the slope above Tophane.

name: Petra Roasting Co., Bebek
notes: The walk north from Arnavutköy along the water, past the wooden yalı, ends in Bebek — and this branch opens at half past seven on weekdays, which makes it the obvious place to put a morning after the best hour on the European shore. It is closed on Mondays, so build the walk around a Tuesday. Four further branches sit at Gayrettepe, Şişhane, Topağacı and Maslak if you are on the wrong side of the hill; the Şişhane one also closes Mondays, the rest do not.
verdict: Where the shore walk ends and the morning's work starts.

name: Kubbeli Saloon, Pera Palace
notes: Vallaury again: he began the hotel in 1892 and it opened in 1895, built to lodge Orient Express passengers arriving off the Paris run. It carried the first electric lift in Constantinople — reportedly the second in Europe — and Atatürk's Room 101 is kept as a museum room. The domed saloon pours a traditional afternoon tea every day from three until six, with live piano. It is priced the way a grand hotel prices things: an hour of reading and correspondence, not a working day.
verdict: Built for people who had just spent three days on a train.

name: The vapur — Şehir Hatları ferry
notes: Şirket-i Hayriye began running boats across the strait in 1851, and until the first Bosphorus bridge opened in 1973 the water was the only way over. Şehir Hatları still works 30 boats on 32 lines between 53 piers, and carried 40 million passengers in 2023. Tea comes round in tulip glasses on a tray that never spills; gulls track the stern for thrown simit. Twenty minutes, both shores lit, no table and no plug — and that is the entire point.
verdict: The best room in Istanbul moves, and costs almost nothing.

name: Pierre Loti Hill
notes: Louis Marie-Julien Viaud, a French naval officer who published as Pierre Loti, turned his Istanbul sojourn into the 1879 novel Aziyadé and spent his free hours on this hill; the house is now a museum under his name. A cable car climbs from the Golden Horn shore to the terrace, which sits above Eyüp cemetery — long a favoured burial ground for its closeness to the tomb of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, over which Mehmed II raised a marble tomb and a mosque after 1453. Tea and nargile, and nothing whatsoever to plug in.
verdict: Tea above a cemetery, the whole Golden Horn laid out below.

name: Çadır Köşkü, Yıldız Park
notes: Abdülhamid II walled the outer garden of Yıldız Palace and filled it with artificial lakes, summer houses and a porcelain factory that is still going. Two of those pavilions, Çadır and Malta, now work as cafés inside what has since become a public park of some 368,000 square metres — breakfast, lunch, or a glass of tea under the trees, run by the municipal operator BELTUR along with the park's other restaurants. The climb from the Beşiktaş gate is steep enough that nobody arrives wanting to open a laptop.
verdict: A sultan's private garden, two pavilions, and a glass of çay.

name: Büyükada
notes: Horse-drawn phaetons were the only transport on the island until 2020, when they were phased out after a serious equine disease and replaced by battery-powered electric vehicles that work like taxi cabs; islanders have since resisted the arrival of buses in the pedestrianised zone. The building everyone photographs, the Greek Orthodox orphanage on the Hristos ridge, went up in 1898 to a design by Alexander Vallaury and is believed to be the largest wooden structure in Europe and the second largest in the world — it took in children until 1964, has stood empty since, and a restoration was annou
verdict: The largest of the Princes' Islands, and the one where the horses were taken away.

name: Heybeliada
notes: The Theological School of Halki was founded in 1844 inside the Hagia Triada monastery and trained clergy for the Ecumenical Patriarchate until 1971, when the Constitutional Court struck down parts of Turkey's private higher-education law; it has never reopened and remains closed to the public. The Naval High School overlooking the jetty was founded in 1773 and holds the Byzantine church of the Kamariotissa and the relocated grave of Edward Barton, Elizabeth I's ambassador to the Porte. The island is 2.35 square kilometres with 4,424 residents at the 2022 count, rising to around 30,000 in high
verdict: The quiet island next door, with a seminary at the top of it that has been closed since 1971 and is still a diplomatic file.

name: Anadolu Kavağı & Yoros Kalesi
notes: Yoros stands above the confluence of the Bosphorus and the Black Sea and changed hands more often than almost any fort in Turkey: the Ottomans took it in 1305 and held it again from 1391 to 1414, the Genoese held it for the forty years to 1454 — which is why locals still call it the Genoese Castle — and Mehmed II refortified it after 1453. It was excavated between 2018 and 2021 and is open to the public again, though the ground immediately around it remains a military area and is closed; the site sits on the UNESCO tentative list. The village below is tiny, 1,517 residents at the 2022 count pl
verdict: The last village before the Black Sea, and the much-conquered castle on the hill above it.

name: Rumeli Kavağı
notes: This is the northernmost settlement on the European side of the strait, and the majority of its 3,560 residents (2024 count) descend from Eastern Black Sea migration — which is what ends up on the plate. The village is known locally for exactly three things: fish, mussels and figs. A Byzantine fortress once stood here and was demolished on Mehmed II's order; excavation has also turned up traces of a Byzantine temple and harbour works beneath the settlement. The catch: nearly every cruise passenger stays aboard for the castle across the water, so there are fewer kitchens open here and no schedu
verdict: Get off one stop early, on the European bank, where the fish is the same water and the audience is not.

name: Hıdiv Kasrı
notes: The Khedive of Egypt — the Ottoman viceroy of a province richer than most of the empire — built his holiday house on this headland in 1907, and it is one of the very few grand houses around Istanbul where you get inside the rooms rather than photographing a façade, because the building now trades as a restaurant and café inside its own public park. The catch is twofold. It is a working hospitality business in a historic shell, so go for the terrace and the grounds rather than for the cooking. And I could not reach a live source to confirm current opening hours in August 2026 — treat the visit
verdict: An Art Nouveau summer palace built in 1907 for the Khedive of Egypt, on a bluff over the Bosphorus.
caveat: Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-15 — call ahead.

name: Polonezköy
notes: Prince Adam Jerzy Czartoryski established the settlement in 1842 for Poles displaced by the failed November Uprising and named it Adampol, a Polish rendering of the Turkish Adamköy; it started with twelve inhabitants and grew through later waves of emigration. Many went home after Poland regained independence in 1918, and those who stayed took Turkish citizenship in 1938. At the 2022 count the village had 346 residents, of whom roughly ninety speak fluent Polish — so what survives is a community held together by memory, a church and a summer festival of Polish folk bands, not a living Polish t
verdict: A Polish village in the Beykoz forest, founded in 1842 by an exiled prince and still holding on to the language.

name: Belgrad Ormanı
notes: The forest takes its name from the Serbs deported here after Süleyman the Magnificent's 1521 siege of Belgrade, settled to maintain the water supply. Two Ottoman systems ran through it: the older Kırkçeşme network, rebuilt by Mimar Sinan under Süleyman, and the eighteenth-century Taksim system, whose Mahmud I aqueduct went up at Bahçeköy in 1732. What you actually walk to are the bents — the dammed Ottoman reservoirs — on a 6.5-kilometre marked track that starts at Neşet Suyu, with seven picnic grounds of which Büyük Bent is the busiest. The catch, and it sends people to the wrong district: Ma
verdict: Five and a half thousand hectares of forest with Istanbul's Ottoman waterworks buried in it.

name: Şile & Ağva
notes: The Şile lighthouse was built in 1859 by French engineers for Sultan Abdülmecid I and lit in 1860 — a 19-metre octagonal tower carrying eight 925-millimetre catadioptric lenses with a range of 20 nautical miles, electrified since 1968 and open to visitors as a historic site. The town also gives its name to Şile bezi, the crimped cotton cloth sold across Istanbul's bazaars, with a fair for it each summer; the fourteenth-century Genoese castle on Ocaklı Ada was renovated in 2015 to widespread mockery for looking like a cartoon. Ağva sits between the Göksu and the Yeşilçay — the name means 'betwe
verdict: Istanbul's Black Sea coast: an 1859 French-built lighthouse, a crimped cotton cloth, and a village between two rivers.

name: Yalova Termal
notes: The springs at Termal, inland from the port, have been in use since Byzantine times; Evliya Çelebi recorded the Kurşunlu Banyo, the Leaded Bath, in the seventeenth century, and the complex was enlarged under Abdülhamid II and again in the Republic's first decades. Down at Yalova stands the Yürüyen Köşk, the Walking Mansion: built between 21 August and 12 September 1929, it was found the following summer to be having its roof damaged by the branches of an old plane tree, and Atatürk ordered the building moved rather than the tree cut. Railway track was laid beneath the foundations, the terrace
verdict: Seventy minutes across the Marmara to springs the Byzantines bathed in, and a mansion that was moved to spare a tree.

name: Bandırma
notes: This is the crossing rather than the destination. From Bandırma two TCDD trains a day run down to İzmir, the 6 Eylül Ekspresi and the 17 Eylül Ekspresi, which makes ferry-and-train the old civilised way between Turkey's two biggest coastal cities. South of the town lies Lake Kuş — Manyas, 'Bird Paradise' — 24,047 hectares, a national park since 1959, added to the Ramsar list in 1998, with 239 recorded bird species.
