The catch is real: I could not load İDO's live timetable to confirm current sailings, sailings on this line are limited rather than frequent, and vehicle rules differ by hull type,
verdict: Two hours across the Marmara to the railhead — the route to İzmir that is not a plane.
caveat: Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-15 — call ahead.

name: Tarihi Kadıköy Çarşısı — Güneşlibahçe Sokağı
notes: The market is not a building, it is a grid of short streets behind Söğütlüçeşme, and Güneşlibahçe Sokağı is its spine — OpenStreetMap maps fishmongers at nos. 1–3, a greengrocer at no. 9, butchers, bakeries and a spice counter inside about eighty metres of each other, with more fish and a butcher's row round the corner on Serasker Caddesi. Buy to the Turkish fishing calendar rather than to a shopping list: commercial fishing runs 1 September to 15 April, so palamut lands from September, lüfer through the autumn and hamsi from late autumn into winter, while between mid-April and the end of Augu
verdict: Five minutes uphill from the ferry: the fish row, the butchers and the greengrocers that feed Kadıköy's own kitchens.

name: Mısır Çarşısı — the Spice Bazaar, and what it is now
notes: Turhan Hatice Sultan, mother of Mehmed IV, commissioned the hall as the revenue arm of the Yeni Cami complex; the court architect Koca Kasım Ağa drew it and it was going up in the last months of 1660, after the Great Fire. There are 85 shops today, and the honest reading is that spice is retreating from them: pre-boxed lokum, pistachio pyramids built for photographs, saffron sold by the gram to people who will never cook with it. One measure of the drift — the Ucuzcular spice house, whose family dates its trade to 1886 and which traded under that name for generations, now runs as Hayfene, sell
verdict: Eighty-five shops under a 1660 vault, and fewer of them sell spice every year.

name: Hasırcılar Caddesi — the working street
notes: Hasırcılar is where the wholesale rhythm survives: coffee roasters, nut and dried-fruit merchants, cheese, pickle and pulse counters, and a fishmonger — OpenStreetMap maps the roaster Kurukahveci Nuri Toplar and the fish counter Taze Balıkçı directly on it, a hundred metres from the bazaar's tourist trade. Quantities here are assumed in kilos rather than gift boxes, prices are lower than inside the hall for the same goods, and nobody presses a sample on you to start a negotiation. The street works on the same clock as the wholesalers: weekday mornings, while the handcarts are still moving, and
verdict: The street the bazaar's own traders shop on, running west from the Spice Bazaar's back gate.

name: Beşiktaş Balık Çarşısı
notes: Beşiktaş keeps its fish trade in the covered block behind the square, mapped in OpenStreetMap as Beşiktaş Balık Çarşısı, and unlike the Beyoğlu row it is still a market before it is a restaurant: whole fish on ice, chalked per kilo, gutted and scaled at the counter for nothing. For anyone provisioning off a Bosphorus berth this is the nearest serious fish counter on the European shore — the argument for it over Kadıköy is simply that you do not cross the water with a cold box. The çarşı around it closes the rest of the list inside a hundred metres: nut and dried-fruit counters, helva makers, a
verdict: The European side's working fish market, wedged into the çarşı two minutes from the ferry.

name: Salı Pazarı and the weekly pazar circuit
notes: Worth correcting before you plan a week around it. The Salı Pazarı that Istanbul cooks mean is Kadıköy's, and it no longer stands where the name is remembered: the İSPARK car park on the old ground is still signed Eski Salı Pazarı Otoparkı, while the market itself is mapped up at Hasanpaşa, out towards Kurbağalıdere. Beşiktaş's own weekly street pazar is recorded in OpenStreetMap as a Saturday market, 08:00–20:00, on the ground north-west of Beşiktaş Meydanı, and Bomonti's semt pazarı runs most days with Wednesday off — so the circuit is Tuesday east, Saturday west. The pazar is where price is
verdict: Istanbul's Tuesday market is Kadıköy's, not Beşiktaş's — and it has moved from where its name suggests.

name: Kadınlar Pazarı
notes: This is a community market rather than a general one: the streets around it were settled by families from Siirt and the south-east, and the shops carry what that kitchen needs — otlu peynir threaded with wild herbs, thick pistachios, isot, comb honey, dried pulses — alongside the büryan ocakları where lamb hangs in pit ovens cut into the floor. OpenStreetMap records unusually long trading here, roughly 08:00–22:00 Wednesday to Saturday, 08:00–23:00 on Sunday and from 09:00 Monday and Tuesday, which makes it the one provisioning stop on the historic peninsula still working after the bazaar quar
verdict: The Siirt quarter's larder, trading under the Valens Aqueduct at Zeyrek.

name: Reşat Balık
notes: The house dates itself to 1941 on its own site and runs two counters: Sahne Sokak No: 8 inside the Balık Pazarı off İstiklal, and Bağdat Caddesi No: 476/c at Bostancı on the Asian side. OpenStreetMap records the Beyoğlu shop as Mon–Sat 08:00–20:00 and Sun 08:00–19:00, which matters — most Istanbul fish counters are done by Sunday lunchtime. Be clear-eyed about the setting: the Beyoğlu fish market around it has thinned into meyhane tables and souvenir stalls, so the row is now more restaurant than market and the fish counter is the reason to walk in, not the atmosphere. It is the closest seriou
verdict: A fishmonger in the Beyoğlu fish market since 1941 — and one of the few that opens on Sunday.

name: Feriköy %100 Ekolojik Pazar
notes: The %100 Ekolojik Pazarlar network lists a Şişli market on Saturday, alongside Bakırköy on Friday and Kartal on Sunday, and describes the model in its own words as a "halk pazarı" — a public market where growers sell direct, not a boutique with a certificate on the wall. Certification is backed by field visits and laboratory analyses, and the market keeps a public-relations stall where the inspection reports and residue results for what is on sale can be read on the spot. This is the practical source for the things a city shop handles worst: raw honey, farm eggs, small-dairy cheeses and butter
verdict: A Saturday producers' market where the residue analyses are on a desk you can walk up to and read.

name: Faruk Güllü
notes: Followed by hand on 15 August 2026: gulluoglu.com.tr answers with a 301 to farukgulluoglu.com.tr, which answers with a second 301 to farukgullu.com.tr. The shopfront brand is now "Faruk Güllü Baklava" while the copyright line on that same page still reads "Baklavacı Güllüoğlu Gıda Sanayi ve Dış Ticaret A.Ş." — the company kept the old name, the sign dropped it. The operating address given is a plant on Fırat Plastik Caddesi in Büyükçekmece, an industrial estate at the far western edge of the city, not a shop in the old town. Güllü is a large family and several descendants trade under names bui
verdict: The counter-lesson: the largest holder of the Güllüoğlu name has quietly stopped putting it on the door.

name: Hafız Mustafa 1864
notes: The house's own About page tells a story of custody rather than bloodline: the ahi guild tradition of Hacı İsmail Hakkı Bey, then Cemil Bey, "son of Hafız Mustafa," trading as Çikolat Cemil, then Hacı Avni Ongurlar taking it on. The same page makes an unusual claim for a sweet shop — that it was the first to make poğaça, the salted breakfast pastry — and counts "159 years," which puts the writing at 2023. It is now a large operation: 19 branches listed, 15 of them in Istanbul (Bahçekapı-Eminönü, Sirkeci, Nuruosmaniye, Beyazıt, İstiklal, Taksim, Pera, Üsküdar, Galataport among them), plus five
verdict: A Bahçekapı sugar house that has become an international chain — go for the pudding counter, not the legend.

name: Hatay Medeniyetler Sofrası
notes: Two Istanbul rooms, both verified from the restaurant's own site: İstiklal Caddesi No:39 in Beyoğlu, opposite the French Consulate, and Nispetiye Caddesi No:18 out in Etiler. Künefe is the Hatay dessert and the reason to end a meal here rather than walk on — shredded kadayıf packed around fresh, unsalted, unaged cheese, baked in a shallow copper dish until both faces are dark, then drowned in syrup at the pass. The only credential the house advertises is a TripAdvisor certificate from 2015, which proves nothing at all; judge it on what arrives. OpenStreetMap places the POI just behind the aven
verdict: Künefe cooked the Antakya way, one street off İstiklal, at a house that came north from Hatay.

name: Ali Muhiddin Hacı Bekir
notes: The company's account: Ali Muhiddin Hacı Bekir came to Constantinople from Kastamonu and opened in Bahçekapı in 1777; three generations of the family served as Şekerci Başı, head confectioner to the Ottoman palace; five generations have kept the Bahçekapı shop, which grew from a single room to 88 square metres by swallowing the spice shop next door. Where to be careful is the invention story. The Oxford Companion to Food is blunt — "although Bekir is often credited with the invention, there is no real evidence for it" — and Persian recipes using starch and sugar predate him by centuries. What
verdict: Istanbul's oldest sugar counter, and the one claim about it that the historians will not sign.

name: Şekerci Cafer Erol
notes: The house trades on "1807'den beri" and describes itself as keeping "İstanbul'un en köklü şekerleme geleneği" — the city's deepest-rooted confectionery tradition. Its catalogue reads less like a dessert menu than an inventory of Ottoman sugar work: lokumlar, akide şekerleri, ezmeler, helva, drajeler, nugat, bal ve reçel. The Kadıköy shop is the anchor and OpenStreetMap places it at Yasa Caddesi 19 in Osmanağa Mahallesi, a two-minute walk from the ferry pier. The house has since opened in Galataport, Ortaköy, İstinye Park, Emaar Square and London, which is exactly why the small Kadıköy counter
verdict: 1807 on the sign, and a Kadıköy counter that still sells hard candy out of jars by weight.

name: Saray Muhallebicisi
notes: Founded in 1935 by Hüseyin Topbaş with a stated aim that has survived on the company's own page in the original wording: "Beyoğlu'nda zarif hanımefendi ve beyefendilere tatlıların en güzelini yedirmek" — to feed the elegant ladies and gentlemen of Beyoğlu the finest of desserts. It took fourteen years to make the move that mattered, relocating onto Beyoğlu proper in 1949. The house now counts 21 branches, around 1,400 staff and more than a hundred flavours, and names bal kaymağı, fresh bread, tea and börek among the things it is known for. The İstiklal Caddesi room is the one with the history;
verdict: A milk-pudding house, not a patisserie — opened in Kasımpaşa in 1935 to feed Beyoğlu properly.

name: Baylan Pastanesi
notes: Opened in 1923 by Filip Lenas, a Greek of Albanian origin, with his cousin Yorgi Kiriçi — first in Deva Çıkmazı under the name Loryan, the Turkish ear's rendering of "Le Orient" — and moved onto İstiklal Caddesi, into the Luvr Apartmanı, in 1928. The Kadıköy branch that most people now mean by "Baylan" was opened in 1961 by Mikail Lenas. The Kup Griye is the house's own: created by Harry Lenas in 1954, vanilla and caramel ice cream under whipped cream, honeyed almonds and caramel sauce, served with a kedidili biscuit. The business passed to the Altınmarka group, owner of Kahve Dünyası, in 2009
verdict: The republic's oldest pâtisserie, and one dessert that was invented inside it in 1954.

name: Mado
notes: The company's own history page traces the thing back to snow carried down from Ahır Dağı above Kahramanmaraş, which "Osman Ağa" enriched with milk, honey and salep. His descendants Mehmet, Atilla and Erdal Kanbur turned it into an industry — Yaşar Kanbur began by making and selling ice cream from a small shop next to the Aras bus garage — with a Kahramanmaraş factory in 1965, machines in 1970, the MARDO brand in 1984 and real modernisation in 1989. The house dates itself to 1850. Two ingredients do all the work: goat milk, which is why the company runs its own "MADO Beyazı" goat farm, and sale
verdict: The Kahramanmaraş ice cream you cut with a knife — and the chain that industrialised it, which is both the point and the limit.

name: Meşhur Dondurmacı Ali Usta
notes: What is actually on record: OpenStreetMap carries a point of interest named "Meşhur Dondurmacı Ali Usta" on Moda Caddesi in Caferağa Mahallesi, Kadıköy, with the telephone +90 216 414 1880 attached. There is no company website, no published hours, and no dated confirmation from any source I trust that the counter was serving in August 2026. That is not a claim it has closed — closure would be a finding, and I do not have one. It is a gap, and the gap is the honest thing to publish rather than a confident pin. Every other entry in this section was checked against a live company website or a fet
verdict: Moda's ice-cream counter, the one every Kadıköy list names — and the one entry here I could not confirm is trading.
caveat: Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-15 — call ahead.

name: Solera Wine Bar
notes: Opened 1 October 2011 on Yeni Çarşı Caddesi and pours only domestic producers — red, white, rosé, sparkling and fruit wine, no imports on the card. Since 2013 the house has farmed its own vineyard at Gaziköy in Tekirdağ, on the Marmara shore of Thrace, and runs its own Şarap Tadımı tasting evenings walking guests through Turkish varieties region by region. This is the room where the argument that Turkey has a wine culture rather than a wine industry gets made in glasses rather than in print. The Thracian producers you will meet here — Chamlija, founded 2007 by Mustafa Çamlıca on the decomposed
verdict: An all-Turkish list in a narrow Beyoğlu room, 300 metres off İstiklal.

name: Sensus Wine Boutique
notes: The Galata room on Büyük Hendek Caddesi was the first; the business now runs thirteen shops across Türkiye, from Kavaklıdere in Ankara to Çeşme, Bursa and İzmir, and says so on its own site. The buying is done on quarterly tasting tours through seven Turkish wine regions, direct from boutique producers, and the same trips bring back the cheese, charcuterie, honey, olives and oil that fill the counter. It is a shop that lets you sit down, not a bar with a shelf — which is why the pairing plate is the point rather than an afterthought. Time Out Istanbul has carried it for years as the Turkish wi
verdict: A stone cellar at the foot of the Galata Tower that sells the cheese as seriously as the wine.

name: Viktor Levi Şarap Evi
notes: Viktor Levi was the son of a Gelibolu sardine family who moved into grapes on Bozcaada, then opened his own şaraphane in Istanbul after the established houses — Pano, Diamandi, İzmirli, Sofaki — refused him a fair price for his wine. He ran it until his death in 1967; his cousin Yasef held it until 1985, then left for America and the doors shut. It stayed closed for fourteen years until Fevzi Büyükerol bought the property in 1999 and spent about a year rebuilding the interior to the original materials and style before reopening it in Moda. The garden behind Damacı Sokak is the reason people st
verdict: A garden wine house in Moda with a founder's story and a fourteen-year gap in the middle of it.

name: Orient Bar, Pera Palace
notes: As of this check the hotel's own page states the Orient Bar is out of service until the end of the summer season, so do not walk up expecting it. What is open in its place is the Orient Terrace on the ground floor, lobby side, over the Golden Horn: 09:00 to 23:00 for the full menu and 23:00 to 02:00 for drinks only. Upstairs, Room 411 is kept as the Agatha Christie room — 46 square metres of period furniture, a library of her books in several languages and a replica of her typewriter, and it is bookable as a guest room rather than roped off as a museum. Smart casual on the terrace; the hotel e
verdict: The lobby-floor bar of the hotel built in 1892 for passengers off the Orient Express — currently dark for the season.
caveat: A limited run — check the end date before you plan around it.

name: Kubbeli Lounge, Pera Palace
notes: The Kubbeli — kubbe is Turkish for dome — is the high-ceilinged salon the hotel built its social life around, and it is the room to use while the Orient Bar is shut. The house lists traditional afternoon tea accompanied by the piano of Aslı Güral, which is unusual: hotels rarely name the musician. Daylight through the high windows is the whole design brief of the room, so it reads completely differently at four in the afternoon than the bar does at eleven at night. It is a hotel salon, priced as one.
verdict: Afternoon tea under the domes, with a pianist named on the hotel's own page.

name: Le Fumoir and C Lounge, Çırağan Palace Kempinski
notes: The hotel runs its drinking rooms as separate registers and publishes the code for each: Le Fumoir takes bar snacks at smart casual, C Lounge is the casual bar, Çırağan Bar handles refined spirits and cocktails at chic casual, and Gazebo is the lobby lounge, an Ottoman-garden conceit with the water in front of it. Tuğra, the palace's Turkish fine-dining room, is the formal end of the same building. Worth knowing before you plan an evening on the European shore: Rüya İstanbul, which appears elsewhere in this guide as a new-wave Anatolian kitchen, is also inside this hotel. The palace was the im
verdict: Two bars inside a nineteenth-century Ottoman palace on the Bosphorus, with a dress code each.

name: The Listening Room at Arkestra
notes: Arkestra occupies a former residential villa built in the 1960s and splits it three ways: the ground-floor restaurant with an open kitchen and courtyard, a 32-cover bistro called Ritmo with its own private entrance and mirrored ceilings, and the Listening Room upstairs. The Listening Room runs a weekly rotation where selectors either pull from the house record collection or bring their own, over craft cocktails, palm-tree feature walls and low tables. The honest catch, stated by the house: it currently welcomes restaurant guests only, so it is not a room you can walk into off the street. Cenk
verdict: A hi-fi room with a wall of vinyl on the upper floor of a one-star restaurant, in a 1960s villa in Etiler.

name: Kontra Plak
notes: Two doors from Galatasaray Lisesi on the street that has quietly become Beyoğlu's record row, Kontra carries new and second-hand Turkish and foreign vinyl, CDs, cassettes and music books in both Turkish and English, plus turntables, cartridges and headshells. Its own site was showing arrivals dated August 2026 when this guide checked, which is the only proof of life that matters for a shop. It runs named strands rather than one-off events — Dinleme Odası, the listening room; Kontra'da; Örümcek; Just Kids — and takes part in Record Store Day with in-store concerts. Context for why this matters:
verdict: An independent record shop trading on Yeni Çarşı since 2012, with a listening-room programme attached.

name: Analog Kültür
notes: It opened on Record Store Day 2014, when DJ and producer Kaan Düzarat went looking for somewhere to move his studio and decided the studio should be a record shop too. His reasoning, in his own words: in late 2013 there were very few shops in the city and none where you could reliably find good electronic music, old or new, so he built a room to share whatever passed his own filter. About eighty percent of the archive is second-hand — 45s and albums from the seventies and eighties, house, techno, drum and bass, synthwave and krautrock from the nineties and 2000s, then jazz, funk, soul, bossa,
verdict: A record shop and studio on a Şahkulu cul-de-sac that also cuts one-off lathe records.

name: Akmar Pasajı
notes: It stands on the site of the Özel Marmara Koleji, a school founded in 1957 whose building was damaged by adjacent construction in 1980, demolished, and replaced in 1982 by an office block with shops on the lower floors. The name is a splice: Akdik, the owning family's surname, and syllables lifted from the school's. It runs through between Mühürdar Caddesi and Neşet Ömer Sokak, which is why half of Kadıköy uses it as a shortcut without ever stopping, and it holds a specific place in Istanbul's fanzine, metal and rock history — enough that in 1999 it was subject to a police raid on unfounded cl
verdict: The Kadıköy arcade that has been the city's second-hand book and record warren since 1982.

name: Kadıköy Plak Kulübü
notes: It sits in the Kadıköy İş Merkezi on Neşet Ömer Sokak — the far end of the same short block that Akmar Pasajı empties into, so the two are one walk. The shop splits its stock plainly: Turkish records, foreign records, rock, plus CDs, cassettes and turntables, and it buys second-hand collections in as well as selling them, which is what keeps the Turkish racks moving. Its own storefront was showing live pricing and current stock at this check. Between this and the arcade you can do the entire Kadıköy record run in under an hour without crossing a main road.
verdict: A working Asian-side record shop, open every day, that also sells the turntable.

name: Tarihi Cumhuriyet Meyhanesi
notes: The house was founded before the Republic was declared and, by its own account, was named by Atatürk himself — take that as the family's claim, not a documented fact, but the table it says he sat at is still kept permanently reserved, and the house has traded under the name since 1923. It is one street off the Beyoğlu fish market on Sahne Sokak, open every day from noon to midnight, with Turkish traditional live music listed as a standing feature rather than a weekend booking. The meze card carries the old Istanbul minority repertoire that most of Beyoğlu has quietly dropped: topik with carame
verdict: A Balık Pazarı meyhane with live Turkish music every night and a table that has been reserved since 1938.

name: Babylon
notes: Time Out Istanbul calls it the city's premier live music venue, and the programme backs it rather than the reputation carrying it: at this check the calendar ran from the Babylon Soundgarden Festival at Bonus Parkorman on 22 and 23 August through Ben LaMar Gay Ensemble on 1 October, Yazmin Lacey on 7 October, Kassa Overall on 9 October, the Samora Pinderhughes Quintet with Elena Pinderhughes on 10 October, Kelly Lee Owens DJ set on 16 October, and Bilal marking twenty-five years of 1st Born Second on 11 December. That is a jazz and left-field booking policy, not a covers room. It sits on Silah
verdict: The city's long-running live room in the old Bomonti brewery quarter, booking hard through winter 2026.

name: Fiba Salon İKSV
notes: Open since 2010 as Salon İKSV in the foundation's Nejat Eczacıbaşı building on Sadi Konuralp Caddesi, it takes the name Fiba Salon İKSV from the autumn 2026 season under a sponsorship with Fiba Grubu. İKSV's own announcement is unusually candid about what the room is for: its chair describes it as where a great many young people first encountered the foundation. The partnership widens the programme beyond concerts into theatre, literature talks, science evenings and jazz-club nights, so the booking pattern you find will not match what the room did five years ago. It is a proper seated hall run
verdict: The İKSV concert hall that has just changed its name for the first time since 2010.

name: KOLI Art Space
notes: Founded 2021 by Elçin Acun and Yasemin Kalaycı. Non-profit production and exhibition space supporting feminist and queer artists, on identity and gender fluidity. Showed at Contemporary Istanbul CI BLOOM 2026.
verdict: An artist-run space with a programme that runs late.
caveat: Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-11 — call ahead.
hot_this_month: Part of the Biennial's 2026 local-initiative programme

name: NOKS (formerly TOZ)
notes: Began 2015 as TOZ, founded by Ece Elder, Elvan Ekren, Sinem Dişli and Volkan Kızıltunç; NOKS after 2018, run by Kızıltunç and Ekren. Showed at Contemporary Istanbul CI BLOOM 2026; SAHA-supported.
verdict: A collective space in Kadıköy, formerly TOZ.
caveat: Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-11 — call ahead.

name: BAS · AVTO
notes: Long-running independent spaces — artist books and experimental programming. SAHA Sustainability Fund supported.
verdict: Artist books and an adjoining project space.
caveat: Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-11 — call ahead.

name: Nublu Istanbul / Nublu Records
notes: İlhan Erşahin's label and room, founded 2005 as the extension of the Nublu sound from New York's Lower East Side. The most internationally connected music operation in the city
verdict: The Istanbul arm of the New York label and club.
caveat: Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-15 — call ahead.
hot_this_month: Istanbul Sessions released their sixth album, Mahalle, on 16 January 2026

name: Sazzou
notes: Built around jazz and cocktail culture — live jazz plus vinyl DJ sets.
verdict: A small jazz room with a live programme.
caveat: Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-11 — call ahead.

name: The sequence, start to finish
notes: An Ottoman bath is one room type repeated: a cold entrance hall, a warm transitional room, a hot room, and a furnace you never see. You arrive into the camekân (also written camegâh), the domed hall, and sign in at reception. You get a numbered key and a cabin, you strip, you wrap. Then you walk into the hararet — the hot room — and lie on the göbek taşı, the raised marble platform heated from beneath, until your skin softens. Kılıç Ali Paşa puts that wait at fifteen to twenty minutes and it is not filler; the scrub does not work on cold skin. Only then does the attendant come. Kılıç Ali Paşa
verdict: Camekân, göbek taşı, kese, foam, rinse — allow ninety minutes to two hours, and do not plan anything after it.

name: What you wear, and the nudity rule
notes: The peştemal — a flat-woven cotton wrap — is the whole costume, and it stays on. Kılıç Ali Paşa states it in writing: it is not permitted to be completely nude on the premises, and you must be covered from the waist down. Galatasaray prints the same rule in Turkish on its booking pages. This is the most common false expectation people arrive with, in both directions: some brace for a nudity ordeal that does not happen, others strip off and get corrected. Underwear or a bikini bottom stays on under the wrap. Zeyrek keeps disposable underwear on hand but still advises bringing your own spare; Sü
verdict: You are not naked. In most of these houses being fully naked is explicitly forbidden.

name: Gendered hours — the way this trip actually fails
notes: There is no single rule in Istanbul. Some baths are çifte — twin buildings under one roof, a men's half and a women's half behind separate street doors. Some are a single bath sliced by the clock, with a dead changeover in between. Some are mixed and take couples and families together. And at least one is currently not serving women at all. Two things bite hardest. First, the last reservation is often hours before closing, so the published closing time is not when you can still turn up. Second, two houses on this list — Cağaloğlu and Galatasaray — describe men's and women's sections but publis
verdict: Four systems across nine buildings, and two houses that do not publish the split at all. Get it wrong and you have crossed a city to a locked door.

name: The money, the extras and the hard sell
notes: Two houses state it in writing and the rest operate the same way: the traditional hammam ritual does not include an oil massage. Kılıç Ali Paşa — 'a traditional hammam ritual treatment does not include a massage. A separate reservation is required.' Galatasaray — the same line in Turkish, asking you to declare it when you book. A massage means a separate room, a separate therapist, a separate booking and a separate bill, and at Kılıç Ali Paşa it costs more than the bath itself (₺4,600 for fifty minutes against ₺4,300 for the ritual). Expect it to be offered warmly while you are wet, wrapped an
verdict: The massage is not in the bath price. It has never been in the bath price. Say no or budget for it.

name: Who should not go in
notes: This is a 40°C room at around 70% humidity with a stranger applying pressure to your body for half an hour, and the houses take the medical side more seriously than most spas. Zeyrek publishes the longest list: hammam services are not recommended for guests with cardiovascular disease, high or low blood pressure, respiratory disease including asthma, bronchitis and COPD, diabetes, urinary tract infection, recent surgery or cancer treatment — and guests with severe skin problems such as burns, allergies, open wounds, or with epilepsy, cannot be served at all. Zeyrek also does not recommend the
verdict: Two of these houses will refuse you at the door, and they are right to.

name: Zeyrek Çinili Hamam
notes: Barbaros Hayreddin Paşa, grand admiral of the Ottoman fleet, commissioned it; the house credits Mimar Sinan, building during the reign of Süleyman the Magnificent, over a Byzantine cistern. The house does not publish a precise construction year on its history page, so treat the commonly quoted 1530s dating as convention rather than something you can source from the owner. The İznik tiles that gave the bath its name were lost long ago and are dispersed among European collections — the specific museums and the often-quoted tallies of recovered fragments and reconstructed patterns are widely repe
verdict: Sinan's bath for the grand admiral, back in service after a thirteen-year restoration — with a museum built into it.

name: Kılıç Ali Paşa Hamamı
notes: Mimar Sinan built this inside admiral Kılıç Ali Pasha's mosque and school complex to serve the levends, the crews of the Ottoman fleet, when Tophane was the working harbour. The house's own two pages date it slightly differently — 1578 to 1580 on one, 1578 to 1583 on another — so take it as late 1570s to early 1580s. The patron is worth knowing: born Giovanni Dionigi Galeni in Calabria, captured and set to work as a galley slave, he converted, rose to command the Ottoman navy, and appears in Italian sources as Occhiali and in Cervantes as Uchali. The hot room is a single great volume under a d
verdict: Sinan built it for the crews of the Ottoman navy. One dome, one bath, and the clock decides whether you are allowed in.

name: Ayasofya Hürrem Sultan Hamamı
notes: Süleyman the Magnificent had Mimar Sinan build this in 1556–57 at the request of Hürrem Sultan, the woman Europe called Roxelana — born in Rohatyn in the Polish crown lands, taken into the harem, and one of very few women formally married to an Ottoman sultan. It sits between Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque, on the site of the ancient baths of Zeuxippus. Its architectural claim is specific and the house states it plainly: seventy-five metres long, and the first Ottoman bath built with the men's and women's halves as mirror images on a single axis — men's cold, warm and hot rooms running into
verdict: Sinan's 1556 bath for Roxelana, built on the Roman baths of Zeuxippus — and priced like the square it stands on.

name: Cağaloğlu Hamamı
notes: Constructed in 1741 under Mahmud I, begun by the architect Süleyman Ağa and completed by Abdullah Ağa, and endowed as a çifte public bath to generate revenue for the sultan's library inside Hagia Sophia. The bath paid for the books. Nothing on this scale followed it in Istanbul — the house calls it the last example of its kind built in the city. The two entrances are on different streets: the men's on the main road, up a staircase of ten steps between two marble columns with classic stalactite capitals, under an inscription of seven lines and twenty-eight verses; the women's on the side street
verdict: The last great bath the empire built — and it was built to pay for a library.

name: Çemberlitaş Hamamı
notes: Built in 1584 for Nurbanu Sultan — valide sultan, and after Selim II's death the effective power inside the palace — with the takings endowed to her Atik Valide complex across the Bosphorus in Üsküdar. The Sinan attribution is conventional but should be held loosely: the house itself words it as 'attributed to Mimar Sinan' rather than claiming it flatly, which is the honest position and rarer than it should be in this trade. A fire in 1865 and the widening of Divan Yolu in 1868 took part of the building, and the great domed changing hall in every photograph of this bath is the men's. The women
verdict: A queen mother's bath, funding a mosque across the water, open eighteen hours a day.

name: Süleymaniye Hamamı
notes: A bath in the Süleymaniye quarter trading on 'Since 1550' and crediting Mimar Sinan, run quite unlike anything else on this list. Note the house's own arithmetic wobbles — its FAQ calls the building 472 years old, which would put it at 1554 rather than 1550 — so take the founding year as approximate. During its main hours it takes only couples and families, together, in a shared communal room, and it will not separate partners once you are in: they state flatly that couples must take the scrub and massage together and that requests to split are not accommodated. Their wording throughout is 'co
verdict: Wood-fired since 1550 — the one place couples bathe together, and the one where every attendant is male.
caveat: A limited run or temporary regime — check before you plan around it.

name: Tarihi Galatasaray Hamamı
notes: Part of the Galatasaray külliye, built with the complex in 1481 under Bayezid II. The house tells the founding story as legend: Bayezid walking the ground where the lycée and the bath now stand, meeting the revered Gül Baba in a hut, asking what he wanted, and being told to build a complex there with a great school and a great domed bath that would outlast centuries. Gül Baba's tomb is still inside the complex. The better-documented detail is later: Fethi İsfendiyaroğlu, who wrote the history of Galatasaray and studied there himself, recorded that in his day the boarders were marched down from
verdict: 1481, inside the Galatasaray complex — and it will not tell you what it costs until you are in the booking flow.

name: Ağa Hamamı
notes: A small bath in the Çukurcuma streets below Galatasaray, with the most transparent pricing in this section: entrance, scrub and foam listed as three separate numbers you add up yourself, with card and cash totals printed side by side. It is a mixed hammam — the house's own history page says it has served as a mixed bath for over a decade — which makes it, with Süleymaniye, one of only two places here where a couple can bathe together. Be clear about what that same sentence says, though: the house describes itself as serving only tourists. This is not a neighbourhood bath and does not claim to
verdict: Mixed, priced in lira, itemised line by line — and well under the Sultanahmet houses for the same three things.

name: Tarihi Üsküdar Çinili Hamamı
notes: Cross to the Asian side for the one bath on this list that is not selling anything. It was built in 1640 for Kösem Sultan as one of four buildings in her Çinili complex — mosque, library, guardhouse and bath — and its original job was washing the masons putting up the Çinili Camii. The house adds a detail worth carrying: Kösem died once the women's section was finished, and her brother saw the construction through. Do not go for the tiles: the İznik work that gave the bath its name was stolen long ago, and the operators used blue stone on the walls instead to keep faith with the original idea.
verdict: 1640, two-metre walls, a tonne of firewood a winter, cash only — and nobody is going to explain anything to you in English.
caveat: Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-16 — call ahead.

name: Tıraş — the full berber
notes: The berber is a licensed trade with its own chamber — the İstanbul Erkek Berberleri Usta ve Kalfaları Esnaf ve Sanatkârlar Odası, whose site was live on 16 August 2026 — and licensed shops display a tarife. That is the point worth carrying: unlike almost everything else in this section, you can ask to see a price list and it is a normal thing to ask. The ear-singeing that finishes the shave is not a stunt for tourists. A flame or a lit wick is run fast over the top of the ear and the cheekbone to take off the fine hair; it lasts two seconds and it does not hurt. The cologne that comes last is
verdict: Cut, cut-throat shave, ear-singe, cologne. A licensed trade, which means there is a printed tariff you are entitled to see.

name: Rimedzo Barber Shop
notes: The shop's own site gives 1986 as its starting year — nearly four decades in the same doorway, three minutes from the busiest tourist square in Turkey, which is the improbable part. What makes it worth naming is not a technique, it is a habit: the site publishes its price list as an image and states plainly that prices may be updated at the shop, which is an unusual amount of candour in this postcode. Knowing the number before the cape goes on is worth more to a visitor here than any particular fade.
verdict: One shop, one back street behind Hagia Sophia, and a price list you are told to look at before you sit.

name: 2.a Berber Barbershop
notes: Most Istanbul shops will shave you with an open razor if you ask; this one sells it as the thing it does, describing itself in its own words as one of the few places in Istanbul to offer a professional hot-towel, cut-throat razor shaving service. It sits on a side street on the slope above Karaköy and publishes its prices in lira with euro and dollar equivalents beside them, which is honest about who walks in. The useful detail for anyone working a boat: by prior arrangement they will come to you, to a flat or to premises, and cut a whole crew in one go.
verdict: One of the few shops in Istanbul that sells the cut-throat wet shave as a named service and prints what it costs.

name: The hamam, and the clock on the door
notes: Most historic Istanbul hamams give men and women the same marble at different hours, and the session times are the single most important thing to check before you cross the city. Kılıç Ali Paşa Hamamı, Sinan's bath of about 1583 for the crews of the Ottoman navy — already covered in this guide's bathhouse section — publishes the split on its own site and it is unambiguous: women 08:00–16:00, men 16:45–23:30. That is the shape of the problem in one line. A woman arriving at five in the afternoon does not get in; a man arriving at eleven in the morning does not either. Süleymaniye Hamamı in Sina
verdict: Four rooms, ninety minutes, and the one thing that goes wrong more than any other: turning up in the wrong half of the day.

name: Sema — ceremony or show
notes: UNESCO proclaimed the Mevlevi Sema ceremony a Masterpiece in 2005 and inscribed it on the Representative List in 2008. What is protected is the ayin — a fixed musical form in four sections, played by a vocalist, a ney player, a kudüm drummer and cymbals — and the turning itself: the left foot planted, the right foot driving the body around it, right palm turned up to receive and left palm turned down to give. The reason an honest question exists at all is legal history. The Republic closed every tekke in 1925, and what survived of the Mevlevi order survived by being reclassified as culture and
verdict: The tennure and the sikke are worn at all three tiers. Nothing about the costume tells you what you have bought.

name: Silivrikapı Mevlana Kültür Merkezi (EMAV)
notes: Evrensel Mevlana Aşıkları Vakfı runs a fixed weekly programme at its own centre and publishes it in English on its own site, which carried a 2026 copyright when I read it on 16 August 2026. The thing that makes this useful to a non-Turkish speaker is specific and unusual: the discourse that opens each evening is a recorded video with English subtitles, so you can follow the evening rather than merely watch it. The centre is associated with Hasan Dede, who spent his life teaching there. There is an ikram — refreshments offered to everyone in the room — partway through, which is the marker that
verdict: A foundation's own sema twice a week, with the discourse subtitled in English and no ticket desk — but you have to phone to find out where it is.

name: Galata Mevlevihanesi
notes: Founded in 1491 and known in Ottoman times as the Kulekapısı lodge, this is the best-known Mevlevi house in the city and the only place a visitor can stand inside a real semahane on an ordinary weekday. It closed with every other tekke in 1925, reopened as a museum in 1975 and was reorganised as the Mevlevi lodge museum in 2011. The hall is the reason to come: a wooden floor, mihrab and minber at the far end, the gallery where the musicians sat, and the side lodges now hung with marbling, calligraphy and hilye sheets. The courtyard tombs include that of the poet Şeyh Galib, who was sheikh here
verdict: A 1491 lodge with a genuine semahane. Visit it as a museum; treat the ceremony as a maybe.

name: Çay bahçesi — the price of a chair
notes: A çay bahçesi is not a café. It is a public room with weather: chairs under a tree, a waiter with a tray, and no expectation that you will ever leave. Tea arrives in a tulip glass — ince belli, thin-waisted — on a saucer with two sugar cubes and a small spoon, poured from a stacked double pot: the demlik on top holds the concentrated brew, the kettle underneath holds the hot water, and the server mixes to your instruction. Açık is pale, koyu is dark, tavşan kanı — 'rabbit's blood' — is the deep red the second glass should be. Grandparents hold tables for four hours over a backgammon board. Stu
verdict: One glass of tea buys the table for as long as you want it. That is the entire contract, and nobody will break it.

name: Nargile — the Tophane strip
notes: Nargile reached Ottoman Istanbul in the seventeenth century and was banned by Murad IV alongside coffee and tobacco on exactly the reasoning he applied to the coffeehouses: men who sit together talk. What is smoked now is mostly mu'assel — tobacco cut with molasses and fruit, sold by flavour. The older thing, tömbeki, is plain soaked leaf fired with raw coal, harsher and slower, still ordered by old men and still available if you ask for it by name. The ritual is entirely about pace: the pipe is packed, the coals are lit and carried over, and a boy works the floor with tongs and a fire tray, c
verdict: If the pipe arrives in under ten minutes it was not built for you. The whole point is the two hours.
caveat: Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-16 — call ahead.

name: Tavla — and whether you can get a game
notes: Tavla here is played fast and loud. The dice are called in Persian — yek, dü, se, cihar, penç, şeş — doubles have their own names, hep yek and dü bara, and the checkers are slammed down rather than placed. A game is over in the time it takes tea to go cold. Every tea garden and every kıraathane keeps boards and lends them for nothing: you say 'tavla var mı?' to the waiter and one arrives with the tea. What does not happen, and travel writing keeps implying that it does, is a stranger sitting down opposite you. A kıraathane is a neighbourhood men's room in which the same four men have been play
verdict: The boards are free and everywhere. The honest answer is that you play with whoever you came with.

name: Katina Fal Cafe
notes: Kahve falı reads what is left after a Turkish coffee. Because the grounds are unfiltered and heavy there is always a residue, and the ritual is to invert the cup onto its saucer — some put a coin or a ring on the base — let it cool, then read the runs of grounds: down the inside walls for what has been, around the rim for what is close, on the saucer for the house. Between friends this happens everywhere in Turkey and costs nothing. Commercially it happens in a specific institution, the fal cafe, and Kadıköy is the city's fal quarter, with several within a few streets of Serasker Caddesi. Kati
verdict: You drink the coffee, turn the cup upside down on the saucer, wait for it to cool, and hand your afternoon to a stranger.
caveat: Not re-confirmed as trading when we checked on 2026-08-16 — call ahead.

name: Türk kahvesi — Fazıl Bey, and the cup turned over
notes: Turkish coffee is judged on the köpük, the fine head of foam, and the foam is a function of heat control: the cezve is brought up slowly and lifted off as it rises, two or three times, and never allowed to boil over. Get that wrong and you are drinking boiled coffee. Fazıl Bey's is the everyday Kadıköy counter that does it properly at an everyday price — a market-side room rather than a set piece, open eight in the morning until midnight, seven days, which makes it one of the few places in this section a chef finishing a shift can actually reach. Sand-brewing — kumda kahve, the cezve set into
verdict: One small cup, twenty minutes, and a foam you can judge the whole thing on.

name: Serpme kahvaltı — the Sunday
notes: This guide already explains what serpme kahvaltı is and where the word came from. What it does not tell you is that it functions as a scheduled event rather than a meal you drop into. The Istanbul version runs on Sunday from roughly ten in the morning to two in the afternoon; tables are held, not turned; and a serious kahvaltı house will not seat two people at a table for four at half past eleven without a booking. The structure matters practically: you make one decision, per person, and then the plates arrive together and keep arriving. There is no second round of ordering, no courses and no
verdict: Twenty plates, three hours, and nothing else planned for the day. It is an appointment, not a breakfast.

name: Rakı-balık — choosing the fish off the ice
notes: The rakı table's spine is cold mezes, then hot mezes, then one fish — and the fish is chosen rather than ordered. In a balıkçı or a meyhane with a counter you walk to the ice at the entrance, point at what you want, and it is weighed in front of you before it goes on the grill. That single step is where visitors lose money in this city more reliably than anywhere else, because the fish is priced by the kilo, the per-kilo price is frequently not posted, and a lüfer that looked like one person's dinner arrives at nine hundred grams. Ask 'kilosu kaç?' before you point, and ask to see the scale. A
verdict: The fish is not on the menu. It is on ice by the door, priced by the kilo you have not yet asked about.

name: Yemek ve Kültür
notes: First issue January 2005; issue 84 is on the table now, four a year, print only, with no overseas subscription offered. Zeynep Dağdeviren is the responsible editor and Musa Dağdeviren sits on the board, filing seven forgotten folk recipes every issue. The advisory board carries Evangelia Balta, the historian of Turkish-speaking Ottoman Orthodox Christians — which tells you how seriously it takes the question of who actually cooked this food.
verdict: The scholarly food journal that grew out of a Kadıköy kebab shop.

name: Vedat Milor
notes: Born 1955, schooled at Galatasaray Lisesi, economics at Boğaziçi, a masters at the LSE and a doctorate in sociology at Berkeley whose thesis the American Sociological Association named the best of 1990. He turned that apparatus on restaurants, first in Milliyet and then in a long-running NTV programme, and edits the English-language Gastromondiale. In Istanbul his verdict moves a booking sheet the way a star does.
verdict: A Berkeley sociologist who became the country's most argued-with palate.

name: Aylin Öney Tan
notes: Her column runs in Hürriyet Daily News, Türkiye's oldest English-language daily, and it is current rather than archival — she was filing through July 2026. Recent pieces have covered gastronomic diplomacy at state dinners, the Culture Route Festival mapping fifty taste stops across Bursa, and the seasonal logic Istanbul kitchens actually work to. The best route into Anatolian regional food without a translator.
verdict: The one Turkish food writer still filing weekly in English.

name: Oggusto and Gazete Oksijen
notes: Between them these two carry the city's rolling new-room lists, and they are usually ahead of the English-language listings. They are different animals. Oggusto is a luxury lifestyle and listings platform, with brand-partnered verticals and a shop sitting alongside the editorial. Gazete Oksijen is a general news weekly — Türkiye, world and economy desks, syndicated New York Times, Financial Times, Economist and Athletic copy — that also keeps a gastronomy section. Neither is a ranked guide. Treat everything as reported, not verified, and assume a share of the rooms will be gone within the year
verdict: Where the openings surface first, and why to read them with a raised eyebrow.

name: Culinary Backstreets
notes: It began as Istanbul Eats, a blog run by Ansel Mullins, who worked in historic restoration, and Yigal Schleifer, then the Christian Science Monitor's Istanbul correspondent. The site first appears in the web archive in April 2009. It has since grown into food tours and reporting across close to thirty cities, but Istanbul remains the deepest desk, and istanbuleats.com now simply redirects here.
verdict: Two men in Istanbul writing up lunch, and they never lost the habit.

name: Cornucopia
notes: Launched in 1992 and made between Scotland, London and Turkey, it now runs two issues a year at a circulation above twenty thousand, edited by John Scott with Berrin Torolsan as publishing director. The register is connoisseurial — architecture, textiles, gardens, Anatolian archaeology — and it treats food as material culture rather than as a booking problem. The complete digital archive of every issue costs about nineteen pounds a year.
verdict: For people who came for the food and stayed for the Ottoman archive.

name: Turkey recap
notes: Independent and reader-supported, written by journalists based in Ankara and Istanbul; the flagship letter launched in 2019 and now runs politics and foreign affairs on Thursdays, business and economy on Fridays. Diego Cupolo co-founded it with Raziye Akkoç. Not a food publication — but licensing, alcohol regulation, inflation and the lira set what an Istanbul evening costs and whether the meyhane down the road can still pour.
verdict: Why the bar you loved is suddenly not serving alcohol.

name: Ottoman History Podcast
notes: Started in March 2011 as an experiment in accessible scholarly production and became one of the largest digital resources of its kind on the Ottoman Empire and the modern Middle East. Chris Gratien, now at the University of Virginia, has recorded more than two hundred interviews. It carries no advertising and takes no revenue, and runs a parallel Turkish-language strand. Search the archive for coffee, wine, famine and the millet system.
verdict: Academics talking properly, without the academic gate.

name: Salt Research
notes: Salt's research library occupies the Alexandre Vallaury building on Bankalar Caddesi that once housed the Imperial Ottoman Bank, and it holds that bank's own archive along with collections on art, architecture and design, and city, society and economy. Much is digitised and searchable from anywhere. Walk out and the Camondo Stairs are a minute away, built in the 1870s by the Ottoman-Venetian Jewish banker Abraham Salomon Camondo.
verdict: An open archive inside the bank that financed the city it later lost.

name: İKSV — Istanbul Foundation for Culture and Arts
notes: It runs the Istanbul Film Festival, the Music Festival, the Jazz Festival, the Theatre Festival, the Istanbul Biennial and the Design Biennial, plus Filmekimi and the year-round Salon İKSV stage, and it curates the Turkish Pavilion at Venice. The calendar and the e-bulletin are the fastest way to learn whether your dates collide with something worth moving a dinner for. Both Turkish and English.
verdict: One foundation programmes most of the big weeks in the Istanbul year.

name: Argonotlar
notes: An independent, deliberately many-voiced contemporary-art platform that began publishing in 2020, named after Maggie Nelson's The Argonauts. It runs criticism, interviews and argument rather than listings, and its ArgAjanda is a working diary of what is open across galleries and artist-run spaces. Turkish only. In a biennial year built around local initiatives, this is how you find out what those initiatives are actually doing.
verdict: The art press that covers the shows the institutions do not.

name: Bant Mag.
notes: First published in 2004 as a monthly print magazine called Bant, it now runs in print and online out of Istanbul across music, cinema, art and illustration, with an online issue archive, a radio and podcast strand, and an English section. The scene it has documented for two decades is the same one that fills the bars on Kadife Sokak — which makes it a listings source by accident.
verdict: The continuous record of what independent has meant here since 2004.

name: Time Out Istanbul
notes: Time Out runs a full local Istanbul edition in both English and Türkçe, across restaurants and cafes, things to do, film, music and nightlife, art and culture. It is a commercial listings operation, not a critical guide, and it should never settle an argument about where to eat. For opening hours, one-off events and what has just appeared in the street you are standing in, it is the quickest English source.
verdict: The English backstop when you need something open tonight.
